stem: A 30 years old female with recurrent sinusitis and persistent productive cough Labs:
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

30-year-old female → young adult with long-standing symptoms

•

Recurrent sinusitis → suggests impaired mucociliary clearance

•

Persistent productive cough → chronic airway infection /
bronchiectasis-type

picture

•

FeNO very low → indicates absence of eosinophilic / Th2-driven airway

inflammation

The most discriminating clue here is very low

FeNO, which essentially excludes

asthma and ABPA.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a congenital disorder of ciliary
structure or

function, leading to ineffective mucociliary clearance.

Why PCD fits this scenario:

•

Impaired ciliary motion → mucus retention → recurrent sinusitis, otitis

media, and chronic productive cough

Symptoms often begin in childhood but may present or be recognised in

adulthood

•

Neutrophilic, non-eosinophilic airway inflammation

o

Hence FeNO is low (key exam clue)

•

Patients commonly develop bronchiectasis over time

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Chronic productive cough + recurrent sinusitis + low FeNO = primary

ciliary dyskinesia (PCD)

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

CVID (Common Variable Immunodeficiency)

•

Causes recurrent sinopulmonary infections

•

Usually associated with:

o

Low IgG ± IgA/IgM

o

Recurrent severe bacterial infections

•

FeNO is not characteristically low nor diagnostically helpful

•

Would expect immunoglobulin abnormalities (not provided)

(Less specific than PCD in this context)

Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)

•

Occurs in asthma or cystic fibrosis

•

Features:

o

High IgE

o

Eosinophilia

o

High FeNO

•

Presents with wheeze, fleeting infiltrates, mucus plugging

(Low FeNO directly contradicts ABPA)

Bronchial Asthma

•

Typically:

o

Episodic wheeze

Dry or minimally productive cough

o

Raised FeNO (eosinophilic inflammation)

•

Persistent productive cough with recurrent sinusitis is atypical

(Very low FeNO effectively rules this out)

Key Points:

• Low FeNO excludes eosinophilic airway disease. In a patient with
chronic

productive cough and recurrent sinusitis, think primary ciliary
dyskinesia.

stem: A 29 years old women presents with 1 year of abdominal bloating & loose stool. H/O urgency & frequency of stool movement in morning. Recently mucus in stool Weight and appetite normal Proctoscopy show small internal haemorrhoids. Most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

•

29-year-old woman → young adult

•

1 year history → chronic symptoms

•

Abdominal bloating + loose stools → chronic diarrhoeal illness

•

Urgency & frequency in the morning → classically suggests inflammatory

bowel pathology

•

Mucus in stool → red flag for colonic inflammation

•

Normal weight and appetite → argues against malignancy or severe
systemic

disease

•

Proctoscopy: small internal haemorrhoids → does not explain mucus,

urgency, or chronic diarrhoea

The key clinical dilemma is IBS vs IBD, and the next step should be a
non-invasive

test to differentiate inflammatory from functional disease.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Faecal calprotectin is the most appropriate next investigation.

Why faecal calprotectin?

•

It is a marker of neutrophil migration into the intestinal lumen

•

Elevated in IBD (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease)

•

Normal in IBS

•

Recommended by NICE and MRCP exam frameworks as the first-line test in:

o

Patients \<40 years

Chronic diarrhoea

o

No systemic red flags (normal weight, appetite)

How it fits this case:

•

Chronic diarrhoea + urgency + mucus → possible early IBD

•

Faecal calprotectin helps decide:

o

Low level → IBS → no endoscopy needed

o

High level → proceed to flexible sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Young patient with chronic diarrhoea and

mucus → do faecal calprotectin

before endoscopy.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Stool culture

•

Indicated in acute diarrhoea, fever, or recent travel

•

1-year chronic symptoms make infection unlikely

Flexible sigmoidoscopy

•

Ultimately required if calprotectin is elevated

•

But not the first investigation in a stable young patient

Anorectal manometry

•

Used for constipation, faecal incontinence, or dyssynergic defecation

•

Has no role in chronic diarrhoea or mucus

Serum inflammatory markers

•

CRP/ESR may be normal in mild or distal IBD

•

Less sensitive and less specific than faecal calprotectin

•

Normal markers do not exclude IBD

Faecal calprotectin is the first-line investigation to distinguish IBS
from

IBD in young patients with chronic diarrhoea and mucus.

stem: A patient presented with features of Crest syndrome ANA 1:160 & Anti-centromere 1:120 Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Features of CREST syndrome

o

C → Calcinosis

o

R → Raynaud's phenomenon

o

E → Esophageal dysmotility

o

S → Sclerodactyly

T → Telangiectasia

•

ANA positive (1:160) → supports an autoimmune connective tissue disease

•

Anti-centromere antibody positive (1:120) → highly specific for limited

cutaneous systemic sclerosis

•

No features suggesting:

o

Multisystem inflammatory disease

o

Overlap syndrome

o

Isolated Raynaud's only

The single most decisive clue is anti-centromere antibody positivity in
a patient

with CREST features.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) is the condition
classically associated

with CREST syndrome.

Why this diagnosis fits perfectly:

•

CREST is not a separate disease → it is the clinical subset of limited

cutaneous systemic sclerosis

•

Anti-centromere antibodies are:

o

Strongly associated with lcSSc

o

Predict:

▪

Long-standing Raynaud's

▪

Digital ulcers

▪

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (late)

•

Skin involvement is typically:

o

Distal (hands, forearms, face)

o

Slowly progressive

•

Renal crisis is less common than in diffuse disease

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• CREST + anti-centromere antibodies = limited cutaneous systemic

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

SLE

•

Associated antibodies:

o

Anti-dsDNA

o

Anti-Sm

•

Clinical picture:

o

Multisystem inflammatory disease

o

Malar rash, arthritis, nephritis

•

Anti-centromere antibodies are not seen in SLE

MCTD (Mixed connective tissue disease)

•

Defined by:

o

Anti-U1 RNP antibodies

•

Features overlap between:

o

SLE

o

Scleroderma

o

Polymyositis

•

CREST features alone + anti-centromere does not fit MCTD

Raynaud's

•

Raynaud's is a symptom, not a diagnosis

•

Does not explain:

o

CREST features

o

Autoantibody profile

Key Points:

• CREST syndrome with anti-centromere antibody positivity is diagnostic
of

limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Cranial nerve involvement may occur (not

mandatory)

Why this case fits GBS perfectly:

•

Time course: days to weeks (1 week here)

•

Pattern: lower limbs \> upper limbs

•

Reflexes: absent

•

Autonomic involvement: postural hypotension (\>20 mmHg is significant)

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Acute flaccid paralysis + areflexia + autonomic instability = GBS
until

proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Syringomyelia

•

Chronic condition, slowly progressive

•

Causes dissociated sensory loss (pain & temperature)

•

Reflexes may be lost at the level of lesion, not globally

•

Autonomic hypotension is not typical

(Time course and reflex pattern do not fit)

Poliomyelitis

•

Now extremely rare

•

Causes asymmetrical flaccid paralysis

•

Reflexes reduced only in affected muscles

•

No autonomic dysfunction

•

Often associated with fever/viral prodrome

(Pattern is wrong and epidemiology unlikely)

Cervical cord compression

A 76 years old male with reduced walking and increased tiredness,

Background history of T2DM, recent diarrhoeal illness.

MRC 4/5 on distal LL, MRC 4+ on proximal LL, normal muscle strength
elsewhere,

absent reflexes, sensory loss in stocking distribution.

Diagnosis?

GBS

Diabetic neuropathy

Mononeuritis multiplex

ANSWERS:

GBS

Correct Answer:

GBS (Guillain--Barré syndrome)

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

76-year-old male → older age does not exclude

GBS

•

Recent diarrhoeal illness → classic trigger (e.g. Campylobacter jejuni)

•

Reduced walking + increased tiredness → evolving neuromuscular weakness

•

Motor findings:

o

Distal lower limbs MRC 4/5

o

Proximal lower limbs MRC 4+

o

Upper limbs normal

•

Absent reflexes → key diagnostic clue

•

Sensory loss in stocking distribution

•

Subacute onset → days to weeks

The most important discriminators are recent infection + symmetrical
weakness +

areflexia

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Guillain--Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory
polyradiculoneuropathy, most

commonly triggered by a preceding infection.

Why GBS best fits this case:

•

Temporal relationship: diarrhoeal illness preceding neurological
symptoms

•

Pattern of weakness:

o

Symmetrical

o

Lower limbs affected first

o

Distal slightly more than proximal (common

early)

•

Areflexia: hallmark feature of GBS

•

Sensory involvement:

o

Often mild

o

Stocking-type sensory loss is common

•

Progressive functional decline (reduced walking)

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Any patient with recent infection + symmetrical weakness + absent

reflexes = GBS until proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Diabetic neuropathy

•

Typically:

o

Chronic, slowly progressive

o

Predominantly sensory

o

Motor weakness occurs late

•

No clear acute deterioration

•

Diabetic neuropathy is not triggered by recent diarrhoeal illness

•

Would not explain subacute decline in walking over a short period

Mononeuritis multiplex

•

Characterised by:

o

Asymmetric

o

Patchy involvement of individual nerves

•

Often painful

•

Associated with:

o

Vasculitis

o

Systemic inflammatory disease

•

Reflexes are lost only in affected nerves, not globally

(Pattern is symmetrical, not multifocal)

Key Concepts:

• Subacute symmetrical lower-limb weakness with areflexia following a

diarrhoeal illness is Guillain--Barré syndrome --- even in patients with

diabetes.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of denosumab?
options: Fully human monoclonal antibody targeting RANKL, reducing osteoclast activity
SERM blocking oestrogen receptors in bone
explanation:
(Receptor

Activator of Nuclear factor Kappa-B Ligand).

Normal physiology:

•

RANKL (produced by osteoblasts) binds to RANK on osteoclast precursors

•

This interaction → osteoclast differentiation, activation, and survival

What denosumab does:

•

Binds to RANKL

•

Prevents RANKL from binding to RANK

•

→ Inhibits osteoclast formation and function

•

→ Reduces bone resorption

•

→ Increases bone mineral density and reduces fracture risk

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Denosumab mimics the action of osteoprotegerin (OPG), the natural

RANKL inhibitor.

MRCP-Relevant Clinical Points

•

Used in:

o

Osteoporosis (postmenopausal, male, steroid-induced)

o

Bone metastases

•

Given as 6-monthly subcutaneous injection

•

Important adverse effects (exam favourites):

o

Hypocalcaemia (especially in CKD)

o

Osteonecrosis of the jaw

o

Rebound vertebral fractures if stopped abruptly

Denosumab inhibits RANKL, preventing osteoclast activation and reducing

bone resorption.

stem: A 78 yr old had Achillis tendon rupture with history of asthma, HTN and multi-drug resistance UTI. On chlorthalidone, Ramipril, ciprofloxacin. What drug caused it?
explanation:
tendinopathy and

tendon rupture, particularly the Achilles tendon.

Mechanism:

•

Fluoroquinolones:

o

Disrupt collagen synthesis

o

Increase tendon matrix degradation

•

This weakens tendon structure, predisposing to rupture

Risk factors that amplify this effect:

•

Age \>60 years

•

Concomitant corticosteroid use (not present here, but classic)

•

Renal impairment

•

High physical stress on tendons

Even without steroids, elderly patients are at significant risk.

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Achilles tendon rupture in an elderly patient on antibiotics =

fluoroquinolone until proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Chlorthalidone

•

Thiazide-like diuretic

•

Adverse effects:

o

Hypokalaemia

o

Hyperuricaemia

o

Hyponatraemia

•

No association with tendon rupture

B. Ramipril

•

ACE inhibitor

•

Adverse effects:

o

Cough

o

Hyperkalaemia

o

Angioedema

•

Does not cause tendinopathy or tendon rupture

Key Points:

• Fluoroquinolones --- especially ciprofloxacin --- are a well-known
cause of

Achilles tendon rupture, particularly in elderly patients.

A 35 years old developed a growth at the lateral canthus of her eye. She
feels

sensation of foreign object in her eye.

On examination, swelling with crusty appearance noted.

What\'s the cause of the swelling?

A. Hemophilus influenza

B. Herpes Simplex virus 1

C. Human papilloma virus

D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

E. Staphylococcus aureus

ANSWERS:

Human papilloma virus

Correct Answer

C. Human papilloma virus

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

35-year-old woman → adult with a localized peri-

ocular lesion

•

Growth at the lateral canthus → eyelid / peri-ocular skin involvement

•

Foreign body sensation → common with surface epithelial lesions

•

Crusty appearance → suggests a papillomatous / verrucous lesion, not
acute

infection

•

No features of:

o

Acute pain

o

Purulent discharge

o

Rapid inflammation

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Human papilloma virus (HPV) is the most common cause of eyelid
papillomas,

including lesions at the canthus

Why HPV fits best:

•

Causes squamous papillomas of the eyelid

•

Lesions are:

o

Slow growing

o

Crusty or verrucous

o

Often cause foreign body sensation

•

Typically, painless

•

Occur on eyelids, canthi, conjunctiva

Common subtypes involved:

•

HPV 6 and 11 (benign epithelial lesions)

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• A chronic crusty growth at the eyelid or canthus with foreign body

sensation is most commonly HPV-related papilloma.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Haemophilus influenzae

•

Causes acute conjunctivitis

•

Presents with redness, discharge

•

Does not cause localized crusty growths

B. Herpes simplex virus type 1

•

Causes:

o

Painful vesicles

o

Ulceration

o

Dendritic corneal ulcers

•

Lesions are acute and painful, not chronic crusty growths

D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

•

Associated with severe keratitis, especially contact lens users

•

Rapidly destructive infection

•

No chronic crusty mass

E. Staphylococcus aureus

•

Causes:

o

Hordeolum (stye)

o

Blepharitis

•

Painful, inflamed lesions, often pustular

•

Not a slow-growing crusty mass

Key Points:

• A slow-growing crusty lesion at the eyelid or canthus, causing foreign
body

sensation is most commonly due to HPV-induced papilloma.

ALTERNATIVE OPINION

A 35 years old developed a growth at the lateral canthus of her eye. She
feels

sensation of foreign object in her eye.

On examination, nodular reddish swelling

What\'s the cause of the swelling?

A. Hemophilus influenza

B. Herpes Simplex virus 1

C. Human papilloma virus

D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

E. Staphylococcus aureus

ANSWERS:

Staphylococcus aureus

Correct Answer

E. Staphylococcus aureus

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

35-year-old woman

•

Growth at the lateral canthus

•

Foreign body sensation → eyelid margin / peri-ocular surface involvement

•

Nodular, reddish swelling → inflammatory lesion rather than
papillomatous or

vesicular

•

No mention of:

o

Vesicles

o

Warty/crusty surface

o

Chronic slow-growing mass

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of eyelid inflammatory
nodular

lesions, including:

•

Hordeolum (stye) -- acute, tender, erythematous nodular swelling

•

Chalazion (early inflammatory stage) -- may also appear reddish and
nodular

initially

•

Angular blepharitis -- commonly affects the canthus

Why Staph aureus fits best:

•

It is the commonest organism causing:

o

Hordeolum (acute infection of eyelash follicle or meibomian gland)

o

Blepharitis

•

Clinical features include:

o

Red, tender nodular swelling

Crusting at eyelid margins

o

Foreign body sensation

•

Lesions are acute or subacute, inflammatory, and often painful or

uncomfortable

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• A red, tender / nodular eyelid or canthal

swelling with foreign body

sensation is most commonly staphylococcal.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Haemophilus influenzae

•

Causes acute conjunctivitis

•

Presents with diffuse redness and discharge

•

Does not cause focal nodular swelling

B. Herpes simplex virus type 1

•

Causes painful vesicular lesions

•

Often with ulceration or dendritic corneal ulcers

•

Not a nodular mass

C. Human papilloma virus

•

Causes slow-growing, warty / papillomatous

lesions

•

Typically flesh-coloured or crusty

•

Non-inflamed, non-erythematous

D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

•

Associated with severe keratitis, especially contact lens users

•

Causes rapidly destructive corneal infection, not eyelid nodules

Key Points:

• A nodular, erythematous swelling at the eyelid or canthus with foreign

body sensation is most commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus.

A renal transplant patient develops linear IgG deposition on biopsy directed against type IV collagen. What is the underlying condition?
A patient's father developed a hereditary disease at age 40. The patient now develops it at age 30. What genetic phenomenon does this describe?
Female with blurred vision 3 years ago and upgoing plantar No RAPD CT normal MRI lesion in spinal cord Dx?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

Female with blurred vision 3 years ago → suggests prior optic neuritis.

•

Now: upgoing plantar → upper motor neuron lesion, pointing towards
spinal

cord disease.

•

MRI: spinal cord lesion → transverse myelitis type picture.

•

No RAPD → at present, optic neuritis is not active.

•

CT brain normal → argues against multiple typical MS plaques.

•

Classic for NMO: recurrent optic neuritis + longitudinal spinal cord
lesions.

Detailed Explanation

•

Neuromyelitis Optica (Devic's disease):

o

Autoimmune, associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies.

o

Characterised by optic neuritis + longitudinally extensive transverse

myelitis (LETM).

o

Often misdiagnosed as MS, but unlike MS:

▪

MRI brain often normal.

▪

Spinal cord lesions are long and continuous, not patchy.

▪

Prognosis worse, requires different immunotherapy (rituximab,

azathioprine).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

MS: Brain MRI usually shows multiple demyelinating plaques
(periventricular,

juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal). Here brain CT/MRI normal → not
typical for

MS.

•

Optic neuritis: Would give RAPD + acute visual

loss, but here vision problem

was 3 years ago, not current.

•

INH (Isoniazid toxicity): Causes peripheral neuropathy, not spinal cord
UMN

lesion + optic neuritis

throat.

C3

ANSWERS:

Immunoglobulins (specifically IgA)

Correct Answer: 1. Immunoglobulins (specifically IgA)

Explanation:

The clinical scenario is classic for IgA nephropathy (Berger's
disease):

•

Onset of hematuria within 1--2 days of a sore throat

➤ (This timing is key --- synpharyngitic hematuria, meaning it occurs
during

or very shortly after the infection)

•

Bilateral flank pain + 3+ blood in urine

➤ Suggests glomerular hematuria (likely with RBC casts)

•

Urine findings: Isolated hematuria, often with mild proteinuria

Abnormal Blood Test in IgA Nephropathy:

•

Raised serum IgA levels are seen in up to 50% of patients

o

This reflects systemic overproduction of IgA

o

However, it's not diagnostic and not always present, but it\'s the
most

likely abnormal blood test in this context

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

C3

Normal in IgA nephropathy

Low C3 is characteristic of post-streptococcal GN, MPGN, or
SLE-related

nephritis

•

ANCA

Seen in vasculitic conditions like GPA (c-ANCA) or MPA (p-ANCA)

Not associated with IgA nephropathy

Summary:

In IgA nephropathy, the most likely abnormal blood test is a raised
IgA level.

Complement (C3) is normal, and ANCA is negative.

ALTERNATIVE OPINION

A patient developed bilateral flank pain along with haematuria 2
months after a sore

throat.

Urine analysis showed blood 3+

What will be abnormal on blood testing?

Immunoglobulins

C3

ANCA

ANSWERS:

C3 (PSGN)

Correct Answer: 2. C3

Explanation:

This is a classic presentation of post-infectious glomerulonephritis,
most likely post-

streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), which is:

•

Common in children and young adults, but can occur at any age.

•

Characterized by:

o

Onset of hematuria and flank pain 1--3 weeks after a streptococcal

infection (e.g., sore throat or skin infection)

o

Tea- or cola-colored urine

o

Urine analysis: hematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts

Abnormal Blood Test:

•

C3 is reduced (hypocomplementemia) in PSGN.

o

Due to activation of the complement system via the alternative

pathway.

o

C3 typically returns to normal within 6--8 weeks.

•

C4 is usually normal.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

•

Immunoglobulins

Serum immunoglobulin levels are not typically elevated in PSGN.

IgA might be elevated in IgA nephropathy, but this case fits post-

streptococcal GN, not IgA.

•

ANCA

Positive in ANCA-associated vasculitis (e.g., GPA, MPA), which causes

pauci-immune glomerulonephritis, not typically post-infectious and
often

no complement drop.

In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, look for low serum C3,
recent infection,

stem: Patient diagnosed with myasthenia gravis, started on Pyridostigmine. What is the mechanism of action?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

•

Diagnosed myasthenia gravis → autoimmune disease affecting the

neuromuscular junction

•

Started on pyridostigmine → first-line symptomatic treatment

•

Question asks specifically for mechanism of action

•

Options focus on acetylcholinesterase (AChE) dynamics

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Pyridostigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

Mechanism:

•

It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for breaking
down

acetylcholine (ACh) in the synaptic cleft.

•

This leads to:

o

↑ acetylcholine concentration

o

↑ duration of action of ACh

o

Improved stimulation of the remaining functional nicotinic receptors

at the neuromuscular junction

Why this works in myasthenia gravis:

•

Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against postsynaptic

acetylcholine receptors

•

Number of functional receptors is reduced

•

Increasing ACh availability partially compensates for receptor loss

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• In myasthenia gravis, treatment is not about increasing
receptors---but

maximizing acetylcholine availability at the NMJ.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Increase synthesis of acetylcholinesterase

•

This would:

o

Increase breakdown of acetylcholine

o

Worsen neuromuscular transmission

•

Completely opposite to what is required in myasthenia gravis

(Incorrect and physiologically counterproductive)

High-Yield MRCP Take-Home Points

•

Pyridostigmine = reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor

•

Improves muscle strength by increasing ACh in synaptic cleft

•

First-line symptomatic therapy in myasthenia gravis

•

Does not alter antibody production (that's immunosuppression's role)

stem: A 50 years old Female presented with weakness in all limbs for one week No past medical history Absent DTR Weakness more marked in lower limbs Postural drop of \>20mmHg Diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

GBS (Guillain--Barré syndrome)

Key Points from the Scenario

•

50-year-old female with acute weakness (1 week) → suggests an acute

neuropathic process

•

Weakness in all four limbs, lower limbs more affected → classic
ascending

pattern

•

Absent deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) → points to a peripheral neuropathy

•

Postural drop \>20 mmHg → indicates autonomic dysfunction

•

No past medical history → reduces likelihood of chronic or structural
causes

The combination of acute onset, areflexia,

ascending weakness, and autonomic

involvement is highly characteristic.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Guillain--Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute inflammatory demyelinating

polyradiculoneuropathy.

Core clinical features:

•

Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness

o

Typically starts in the lower limbs and ascends

•

Areflexia or hyporeflexia (essential diagnostic clue)

•

Autonomic dysfunction

o

Postural hypotension

o

Cardiac arrhythmias

o

Urinary retention

•

Sensory symptoms may be mild or absent

Cranial nerve involvement may occur (not mandatory)

Why this case fits GBS perfectly:

•

Time course: days to weeks (1 week here)

•

Pattern: lower limbs \> upper limbs

•

Reflexes: absent

•

Autonomic involvement: postural hypotension (\>20 mmHg is significant)

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Acute flaccid paralysis + areflexia + autonomic instability = GBS
until

proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Syringomyelia

•

Chronic condition, slowly progressive

•

Causes dissociated sensory loss (pain & temperature)

•

Reflexes may be lost at the level of lesion, not globally

•

Autonomic hypotension is not typical

(Time course and reflex pattern do not fit)

Poliomyelitis

•

Now extremely rare

•

Causes asymmetrical flaccid paralysis

•

Reflexes reduced only in affected muscles

•

No autonomic dysfunction

•

Often associated with fever/viral prodrome

(Pattern is wrong and epidemiology unlikely)

Cervical cord compression

Produces upper motor neuron signs below the lesion

o

Hyperreflexia

o

Spasticity

o

Sensory level

•

Autonomic features relate to bladder/bowel, not postural BP drop

(Absent DTRs rule this out)

Key Points:

• Acute ascending weakness with areflexia and autonomic instability is

Guillain--Barré syndrome until proven otherwise.

Safe in pregnancy (including first trimester)

Pyelonephritis

Pregnant patients

Systemic or upper urinary tract involvement

Aminoglycoside

Risk of fetal ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity

Fluoroquinolone

Musculoskeletal adverse effects

stem: A 52 years old female patient presents with malaise, low grade fever, diarrhoea for 8 months after renal transplant. Currently on prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate. Creatinine 1 week ago was 110. O/E: Temp 38.1, PR 97 bpm, BP 140/60 mmHg, mild tender over kidney allograft, Urinalysis normal, Hb 135, WBC 3.5, Platelets 190, Urea 9, Creatinine 130, ALT 110. Investigation?
explanation:
Correct Answer

CMV PCR

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

52-year-old renal transplant recipient → immunosuppressed, high
infection

risk

•

8 months post-transplant → classic window for

opportunistic infections,

especially CMV

•

Current immunosuppression: prednisolone + tacrolimus + mycophenolate →

strong CMV risk

Chronic symptoms (8 months):

o

Malaise

o

Low-grade fever

o

Chronic diarrhoea

•

Laboratory clues:

o

Leukopenia (WBC 3.5) → viral marrow suppression

o

Raised ALT (110) → hepatitis pattern

o

Mild rise in creatinine (110 → 130)

•

Urinalysis normal → argues against bacterial UTI or BK nephropathy

The constellation of chronic diarrhoea + fever + leukopenia +
transaminitis in a

transplant patient is a classic CMV picture.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is one of the most common and serious

opportunistic infections after solid-organ transplantation.

Why CMV fits perfectly here:

•

Timing: typically occurs 1--12 months post-transplant

•

Systemic features:

o

Fever

o

Malaise

•

Organ involvement:

o

GI tract → chronic diarrhoea

o

Liver → raised ALT

•

Haematological clue:

o

Leukopenia (very characteristic)

•

Can also cause CMV allograft nephritis, explaining the mild creatinine
rise

Best diagnostic test:

•

CMV PCR (quantitative viral load)

o

Confirms diagnosis

o

Guides treatment response

o

MRCP-favourite investigation

MRCP Syndrome pearl

Transplant patient + diarrhoea + leukopenia + transaminitis = CMV until

proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

BK virus PCR

•

Causes BK virus nephropathy

•

Presents with:

o

Rising creatinine

o

Often normal systemic features

•

Does not cause diarrhoea, fever, or transaminitis

•

Urinalysis often shows abnormalities

Blood culture

•

Useful in acute sepsis

•

This patient has:

o

Chronic symptoms (8 months)

o

No septic shock

o

Normal urinalysis

•

Does not explain leukopenia + diarrhoea pattern

Serum tacrolimus concentration

•

Tacrolimus toxicity causes:

o

Nephrotoxicity

o

Tremor, hypertension

•

Does not cause diarrhoea, fever, leukopenia, or raised ALT

•

Creatinine rise is mild and not isolated

Stool culture

•

Used for acute infectious diarrhoea

•

Chronic diarrhoea in immunosuppressed patients is more likely viral
(CMV)

• In renal transplant patients, CMV presents with fever, diarrhoea,

leukopenia, and transaminitis --- diagnose with CMV PCR.

stem: A 45 years old with worsening generalised itchiness, H/O well controlled Crohn\'s disease. Not taking any medication. ALT 67, ALP 360, GGT 120, USG Abd: Normal Most likely cause of itchiness?
explanation:
disease

characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the intrahepatic and
extrahepatic bile

ducts.

Why PSC fits perfectly here:

•

Strong association with IBD

o

Classically ulcerative colitis, but also seen in Crohn's disease

•

Symptoms:

o

Pruritus (often prominent)

o

Fatigue

•

Biochemistry:

o

Disproportionately raised ALP and GGT

o

Mild transaminase elevation

Ultrasound may be normal early

o

Diagnosis usually confirmed with MRCP (beading of bile ducts)

• IBD + cholestatic LFTs + pruritus + normal ultrasound = PSC until

otherwise.

Choledocholithiasis

•

Causes extrahepatic biliary obstruction

Ultrasound would typically show:

o

Dilated bile ducts

o

Gallstones

Usually presents with colicky pain ± jaundice

•

Normal ultrasound makes this unlikely

•

Causes isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia

•

Liver enzymes (ALT, ALP, GGT) are normal

Does not cause pruritus

Occurs predominantly in middle-aged women

Strongly associated with anti-mitochondrial

antibodies

Not associated with Crohn's disease

Targets small intrahepatic bile ducts only

Steatohepatitis

•

Produces a hepatocellular pattern

o

Raised ALT \> ALP

Pruritus is uncommon

No cholestatic dominance

stem: Renal transplant patient with recurrent gout is to be started on allopurinol. Which immunosuppressant is dangerous to combine with allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor)?
explanation:

Why azathioprine is contraindicated:

•

Azathioprine is a prodrug → converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP)

•

6-MP is normally metabolized by xanthine oxidase

•

Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase

•

Result → accumulation of 6-MP

•

Leads to:

o

Severe bone marrow suppression

o

Life-threatening pancytopenia

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Allopurinol + azathioprine = profound myelotoxicity (NEVER prescribe

together).

(If unavoidable, azathioprine dose must be reduced to \~25%, but this is
specialist-level

care and exam answer remains "avoid".)

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

b\. Ciclosporin

•

Can increase serum uric acid and precipitate gout

•

Allopurinol may increase ciclosporin levels slightly

Not contraindicated

•

Used together in practice with monitoring

c\. MMF (Mycophenolate mofetil)

•

Metabolized via glucuronidation

•

No interaction with xanthine oxidase

•

Safe with allopurinol

d\. Tacrolimus

•

Metabolized via CYP3A4

•

No interaction with allopurinol

•

Commonly co-prescribed in transplant patients

Key Points:

• Never prescribe allopurinol with azathioprine due to risk of fatal
bone

marrow suppression.

stem: A 42 years old female presents with anxiety, poor concentration. H/O mastectomy for breast cancer. Constant worries. Worry about children if she die. Management?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Sertraline

Key Points from the Scenario

•

42-year-old female → adult with psychological symptoms

•

Persistent anxiety and poor concentration → core features of an anxiety

disorder

•

Constant worries, including future-oriented worries (children, death) →

hallmark of Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD)

•

History of mastectomy for breast cancer → major life stressor, increases
risk

of anxiety disorders

•

No features of:

o

Psychosis (no delusions/hallucinations)

o

Mania

o

Acute panic attacks

o

Short-lived situational anxiety

The key phrase is "constant worries", especially about multiple domains,
over time.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Sertraline, an SSRI, is first-line pharmacological treatment for
Generalised

Anxiety Disorder (GAD).

Why sertraline is the best choice:

•

Treats core anxiety symptoms, not just physical manifestations

•

Effective for:

o

Excessive worry

o

Poor concentration

o

Psychological distress

•

Non-addictive, safe for long-term use

Particularly appropriate in patients with:

o

Chronic anxiety

o

Health-related fears following serious illness (e.g. cancer)

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Persistent, uncontrollable worry across multiple life areas = GAD →
treat

with an SSRI.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Carbamazepine

•

Mood stabiliser / anticonvulsant

•

Used in:

o

Epilepsy

o

Bipolar disorder

•

No role in primary anxiety disorders

Diazepam

•

Benzodiazepine

•

Provides short-term symptomatic relief only

•

Risks:

o

Dependence

o

Tolerance

o

Cognitive impairment

•

Not first-line for chronic anxiety

Propranolol

•

Useful for performance anxiety

•

Controls physical symptoms (tremor, palpitations)

•

Does not treat psychological worry

Risperidone

Antipsychotic

•

Used for:

o

Psychosis

o

Severe agitation

•

No evidence of psychotic symptoms here

• Generalised Anxiety Disorder is treated first-line with SSRIs such as

sertraline---not benzodiazepines.

commonly

Large, polygonal ("fish-scale") scales

Usually, non-inflammatory

o

Inflammatory

o

Very itchy

A cutaneous T-cell lymphoma

•

Affects:

o

Scalp

o

Face

o

Chest

Well-demarcated plaques

stem: Pericarditis. ECG: Widespread ST elevation. What else will it show in acute phase?
explanation:
Correct Answer

PR depression

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Diagnosis: Acute pericarditis

•

ECG already shows widespread ST elevation → classic stage 1 pericarditis

change

•

Question asks: what else is seen in the acute phase

•

This is a pure ECG pattern-recognition question (very high-yield for
MRCP)

Once widespread concave ST elevation is identified, the next associated
ECG clue

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

In acute pericarditis, ECG changes classically evolve through four
stages.

Stage 1 (Acute phase) -- hours to days

•

Widespread concave ST elevation

•

PR segment depression

o

Due to atrial involvement and pericardial inflammation

o

Best seen in:

▪

Limb leads

▪

Left precordial leads

•

Reciprocal PR elevation in aVR

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• PR depression is the most specific ECG feature of acute pericarditis
and

helps differentiate it from MI.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

B -- T wave inversion

•

Occurs in Stage 3 of pericarditis

•

Appears after ST segments normalize

•

Not an acute phase feature

C -- ST depression

•

Seen in:

o

Myocardial infarction (reciprocal changes)

o

Subendocardial ischaemia

•

Pericarditis causes ST elevation, not depression (except aVR/V1)

D -- Prolonged QT

•

Not a feature of pericarditis

Seen in:

o

Electrolyte abnormalities

o

Drug effects

o

Congenital long QT syndromes

E -- Short PR interval

•

Seen in pre-excitation syndromes (e.g. WPW)

•

Pericarditis causes PR depression, not shortening

Key Points:

• Acute pericarditis ECG = widespread ST elevation + PR depression

E -- If asymptomatic hypoglycaemia occurs while asleep, it does not
prohibit

driving

(i.e. nocturnal asymptomatic hypoglycaemia does not stop him from
driving)

N.B.: Although option E is phrased negatively, it is testing the DVLA
rule that

asymptomatic nocturnal hypoglycaemia does NOT restrict driving. This is
the

intended correct concept

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

18-year-old male → new driver, DVLA rules apply strictly

•

On insulin → higher risk of hypoglycaemia

•

Question focuses on fitness to drive, not diabetes control

•

MRCP commonly tests:

o

Severe hypoglycaemia

o

Hypoglycaemia unawareness

o

Nocturnal vs daytime hypoglycaemia

The crucial discriminator is whether hypoglycaemia affects driving
safety.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

According to DVLA (UK) guidance for Group 1 drivers (cars /
motorcycles):

A patient on insulin may drive if:

•

They have good hypoglycaemia awareness

•

No severe hypoglycaemia (requiring third-party assistance) in the last
12

months

•

They check blood glucose before driving

•

They do not have hypoglycaemia unawareness

Key DVLA exam rule

Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia occurring during sleep does NOT count as a

driving-relevant hypoglycaemic episode.

Therefore:

•

No restriction on driving

•

DVLA does NOT need to be informed

•

Patient can start driving

MRCP syndrome pearl:

• Only hypoglycaemia that could impair driving (severe or unrecognised

while awake) restricts driving.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

A. Can start immediately after hypoglycaemia controlled

•

DVLA rules are not time-based

•

Focus is on severity and awareness, not "control"

B. After 1 week

•

Arbitrary time frame

•

No DVLA rule supporting this

C. After 4 weeks

•

Also, arbitrary

•

Applies neither to hypoglycaemia nor insulin use

D. DVLA should be informed after every hypoglycaemia episode

•

DVLA is informed only if:

o

Severe hypoglycaemia

o

Hypoglycaemia unawareness

•

Mild or nocturnal asymptomatic episodes do NOT require notification

Key Points:

• In insulin-treated patients, only severe hypoglycaemia or
hypoglycaemia

unawareness restricts driving.

• Asymptomatic nocturnal hypoglycaemia does NOT.

stem: A 38 years old female came with vivid dreams and occasional crying spells. After traveling to Kenya has broken up with her boyfriend one week back. No regular medications only mefloquine prophylaxis. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer

A. Mefloquine toxicity

Key Points from the Scenario

•

38-year-old female

•

Recent travel to Kenya → malaria prophylaxis relevant

•

Only medication: mefloquine → key pharmacological clue

•

Vivid dreams → classic, highly characteristic adverse effect of
mefloquine

•

Occasional crying spells, anxiety-type symptoms

•

Short time course (1 week) → acute onset

Recent psychosocial stressor (break-up) present, but symptoms are

disproportionate and drug-specific

The single most discriminating clue here is vivid dreams in a patient
taking

mefloquine.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Mefloquine is an antimalarial commonly associated with neuropsychiatric
adverse

effects.

Neuropsychiatric side effects (MRCP high-yield):

•

Vivid dreams / nightmares (very characteristic)

•

Anxiety

•

Mood changes

•

Depression

•

Emotional lability (crying spells)

•

Insomnia

•

In severe cases: psychosis or suicidal ideation

Why this is mefloquine toxicity:

•

Symptoms started after starting prophylaxis

•

No prior psychiatric history mentioned

•

Symptoms are mild to moderate, not meeting criteria for a primary
psychiatric

disorder

•

Time course is acute, consistent with drug adverse effects

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Vivid dreams + travel history + mefloquine = mefloquine toxicity until

proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

B. Drug-induced psychosis

Would present with:

o

Delusions

o

Hallucinations

o

Severe behavioural disturbance

•

This patient has no psychotic features

C. Depressive disorder

•

Requires:

o

Persistent low mood

o

Anhedonia

o

Symptoms for ≥2 weeks

•

This presentation is:

o

Acute

o

Drug-related

o

Lacks core depressive features

D. Bipolar disorder

•

No history of:

o

Mania or hypomania

o

Elevated mood, reduced sleep, grandiosity

•

Acute onset linked to medication, not mood

cycling

E. Adjustment disorder

•

Occurs in response to psychosocial stress

•

Symptoms are usually:

o

Mild

o

Non-specific

•

Does not cause vivid dreams, which are a drug-specific adverse effect

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Mefloquine commonly causes vivid dreams and mood changes---these

neuropsychiatric symptoms should always be attributed to drug toxicity

Female on doxycycline for Lyme disease developed fever, rigors 3 hrs
later.

Jarisch-herxheimer reaction to doxycycline.

How to manage?

Stop doxycycline

Reassurance

Steroid

Plasmapheresis

ANSWERS:

Reassurance

Correct Answer

Reassurance

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Female on doxycycline for Lyme disease

•

Developed fever and rigors within 3 hours of starting treatment

•

This rapid onset after initiating antibiotics is classic for a
Jarisch--Herxheimer

reaction

•

Occurs due to rapid lysis of spirochetes (Borrelia) → cytokine release

•

This is a self-limiting inflammatory reaction, not drug allergy or
treatment

failure

The timing (within hours) and systemic flu-like symptoms are the key

discriminators.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

The Jarisch--Herxheimer reaction is an acute inflammatory response seen
after

starting antibiotics for spirochaetal infections, including:

•

Lyme disease

•

Syphilis

•

Leptospirosis

•

Relapsing fever

Pathophysiology (MRCP-relevant):

•

Antibiotic kills spirochetes rapidly

•

Release of endotoxin-like products

•

Cytokine surge (TNF-α, IL-6)

•

Results in:

o

Fever

o

Rigors

o

Myalgia

o

Headache

o

Transient hypotension (occasionally)

Management:

•

Continue antibiotics

•

Provide reassurance

•

Supportive care (fluids, antipyretics)

•

Reaction usually settles within 24 hours

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Jarisch--Herxheimer reaction is expected, self-limiting, and NOT an

indication to stop antibiotics.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Stop doxycycline

•

Incorrect

•

Would risk undertreatment of Lyme disease

•

Reaction is not a drug allergy

(Never stop antibiotics for Jarisch--Herxheimer

Steroid

•

Not routinely required

•

Reserved only for severe reactions (e.g. neurosyphilis,
pregnancy-related

syphilis complications)

•

Lyme-related reactions are usually mild

Plasmapheresis

•

No role whatsoever

•

Used in immune-mediated conditions (e.g. TTP, myasthenic crisis)

Key Points:

• Jarisch--Herxheimer reaction after treating spirochetal infections is

managed with reassurance and supportive care---antibiotics must be

continued.

stem: What to check once weekly in patient taking linezolid?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Patient taking linezolid

•

Question asks: what should be checked once weekly

•

Linezolid is commonly used for:

o

MRSA

o

VRE

•

MRCP frequently tests drug-specific monitoring requirements

The stem is testing awareness of linezolid's major dose- and
duration-related

toxicity.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein
synthesis by

binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit.

Key adverse effect (high-yield):

•

Bone marrow suppression, especially:

o

Thrombocytopenia

o

Anaemia

o

Leukopenia

•

Risk increases with:

o

Treatment \> 7--10 days

o

Renal impairment

o

Elderly patients

Therefore:

•

Weekly CBC monitoring is mandatory

•

Early detection prevents:

o

Bleeding complications

Severe pancytopenia

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Any patient on linezolid for more than a few days requires weekly full

blood count monitoring.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

CRP

•

Marker of inflammation or infection response

•

Not a toxicity marker

•

No role in monitoring linezolid adverse effects

Magnesium

•

Important for drugs like:

o

Cisplatin

o

PPIs

•

Linezolid does not cause hypomagnesaemia

Electrolytes

•

Linezolid does not significantly affect:

o

Sodium

o

Potassium

•

Electrolyte monitoring is not routine

Key Points:

• Linezolid causes bone marrow suppression --- check CBC weekly.

A 72 years old female on terminal stage non-small cell carcinoma
presented with

haemoptysis

She war on palliative treatment for her locally metastasis cancer.

Immediate next step?

Bloud Transfusion

Dexamethasone

Midazolam

ANSWERS:

Midazolam

Correct Answer:

Midazolam

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

72-year-old female with terminal-stage non-small cell lung carcinoma

•

Known locally metastatic disease

•

On palliative care → goal is comfort, not life prolongation

•

Presentation with haemoptysis → distressing, frightening terminal event

•

Question asks for immediate next step, not definitive oncological or
curative

management

The most important determinant here is

palliative intent.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

In a terminally ill patient, haemoptysis is a catastrophic and highly
distressing

symptom, both for the patient and family.

Why midazolam is the correct immediate step:

•

Midazolam is a benzodiazepine used in palliative care for:

o

Acute anxiety

o

Dyspnoea-related distress

o

Terminal agitation

•

It provides:

o

Rapid anxiolysis

o

Sedation

o

Relief from air hunger and panic

•

It is the first-line drug in catastrophic events (e.g. massive
haemoptysis,

terminal dyspnoea) in palliative settings

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• In terminal haemoptysis, the priority is relief of distress, not
correction of

physiology.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Blood transfusion

•

Not an immediate intervention for haemoptysis

•

Does not relieve distress

•

No role in terminal catastrophic bleeding

•

Inconsistent with palliative goals

Dexamethasone

•

Useful for:

o

Spinal cord compression

o

Cerebral metastases

o

Raised intracranial pressure

•

Not effective acutely for haemoptysis-related distress

Key Points:

In terminal cancer patients with catastrophic haemoptysis, immediate

management is palliative sedation with midazolam to relieve distress.

stem: An 18 year old man with 3 month H/O non-itchy suprapubic rash, small pearly umbilicated papule. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

18-year-old man → sexually active age group

•

3-month history → chronic, indolent course

•

Non-itchy rash → excludes inflammatory or infestational causes

•

Suprapubic location → common site for sexually transmitted skin
conditions

•

Small pearly papules with central umbilication → pathognomonic
description

The single most diagnostic clue is the phrase "pearly umbilicated
papule."

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Molluscum contagiosum is a benign viral skin infection caused by a
poxvirus.

Typical features (MRCP high-yield):

•

Dome-shaped, pearly papules

•

Central umbilication

•

Usually, non-itchy and painless

•

In adults, commonly affects:

o

Genital and suprapubic areas

o

Transmitted via skin-to-skin / sexual contact

•

Lesions persist for months if untreated

Why this fits perfectly:

•

Exact lesion morphology described

•

Correct anatomical location

•

Chronic, asymptomatic nature

•

Classic exam stem wording

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Umbilicated pearly papules = Molluscum contagiosum until proven

otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Lichen planus

•

Intensely itchy

•

Violaceous, flat-topped papules

•

Wickham striae may be seen

•

Not umbilicated

Dermoid cyst

Deep, subcutaneous lump

•

Not papular or multiple

•

Congenital, slow-growing

•

No umbilication

Chronic folliculitis

•

Involves hair follicles

•

Often pustular and inflamed

•

Usually itchy or tender

•

No central umbilication

Pediculosis

•

Causes intense itching

•

Visible lice or nits

•

Excoriations common

•

No papular umbilication

Key Points:

• A chronic, non-itchy, pearly umbilicated papule in the suprapubic
region is

diagnostic of molluscum contagiosum.

stem: A 29 years old female with 9 month back pain, stiffness. The pain localizes to back and stiffness can last for 3 hours and make her wake in morning. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

29-year-old female → young adult (typical age for inflammatory back pain

onset)

•

9 months of back pain → chronic (\>3 months)

•

Marked morning stiffness lasting \~3 hours → strong inflammatory feature

•

Pain wakes her from sleep in early morning → classic for inflammatory
back

pain

•

Symptoms improve with movement (implied by morning stiffness pattern)

The duration, timing, and inflammatory nature of stiffness are the
decisive clues.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Ankylosing spondylitis is a form of axial spondyloarthritis
characterized by

inflammatory back pain.

Hallmarks of inflammatory back pain (MRCP high-yield):

•

Onset before age 40

•

Insidious onset

•

Morning stiffness \>30--60 minutes (often hours)

•

Improves with exercise, not rest

•

Night pain with improvement on getting up

This patient meets multiple criteria:

•

Young age

Chronic back pain

•

Prolonged morning stiffness (3 hours)

•

Night/early-morning awakening due to pain

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Prolonged morning stiffness and night pain in a young adult =

inflammatory back pain → think ankylosing spondylitis.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Fibromyalgia

•

Widespread musculoskeletal pain

•

Associated with fatigue, poor sleep, cognitive symptoms

•

No prolonged morning stiffness

•

Pain does not wake patients due to inflammation

•

Examination typically normal (tender points, not stiffness)

Piriformis syndrome

•

Localized buttock pain

•

Sciatic nerve irritation

•

Pain is mechanical, posture-related

•

No prolonged morning stiffness or night pain

Key Points:

• Chronic back pain in a young adult with prolonged morning stiffness
and

night pain is ankylosing spondylitis until proven otherwise.

stem: Most medial to right internal jugular vein in neck?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Question tests neck anatomy relationships, a

classic MRCP Part 1 SBA

•

Focus is the right internal jugular vein (IJV) and what lies most medial
to it

•

Requires recalling the carotid sheath arrangement and midline neck

structures

The key is understanding relative medial--lateral positioning, not just
what lies next

to the vein.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

In the neck, structures are arranged as follows (from lateral → medial):

Internal Jugular Vein → Common Carotid Artery → Trachea

•

The internal jugular vein lies lateral

•

The common carotid artery lies medial to the IJV

•

The trachea is a midline structure, therefore more medial than both

•

On the right side, the trachea remains the most medial structure
relative to

the right IJV

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• The trachea is always a midline structure and is more medial than the

carotid sheath contents.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Oesophagus

•

Lies posterior to the trachea

•

Slightly deviates to the left, not purely medial to the right IJV

Phrenic nerve

•

Runs anterior to scalenus anterior

•

Lies lateral, not medial, to the carotid sheath

Cervical chain (sympathetic chain)

•

Lies posterior to the carotid sheath

•

Not medial

Common carotid artery

•

Lies medial to the IJV

•

But not the most medial structure overall

(Trachea lies further medially)

Key Points:

• Relative to the right internal jugular vein, the trachea is the most
medial

structure in the neck.

Structure medial to right internal jugular vein?

Oesophagus

Trachea

Phrenic nerve

Cervical chain

Common carotid artery

ANSWERS:

Common carotid artery

Correct Answer:

Common carotid artery

Key Points from the Question:

•

The question asks "structure medial to the right internal jugular vein"

•

It is not asking for the most medial structure overall, only the
immediate

medial relation

The key is to recall the carotid sheath arrangement.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Within the carotid sheath, structures are

arranged from lateral → medial as:

Internal Jugular Vein → Common Carotid Artery → Vagus Nerve (posterior)

Therefore:

•

The common carotid artery lies medial to the internal jugular vein

•

This relationship is constant and clinically important (e.g. central
line insertion)

IJV is lateral, common carotid artery is medial --- always remember
"VAN"

(Vein, Artery, Nerve).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Oesophagus

•

Lies posterior to the trachea

•

Deviates slightly to the left

•

Not directly medial to the right IJV

Trachea

•

A midline structure

•

Medial to both carotid sheaths, but not the immediate medial neighbour

•

The question asks structure medial to IJV, not most medial in neck

Phrenic nerve

•

Runs on anterior scalene muscle

•

Lies lateral to the carotid sheath

Cervical sympathetic chain

•

Lies posterior to the carotid sheath

•

Not medial

Key Points:

• Medial to the internal jugular vein = common carotid artery.

A 70 years old with 1 year progressive breathlessness Worked on a farm
for most of

his life.

O/E: Widespread inspiratory crackles

OXR: diffuse alveolar shadowing

How differentiate farmer's lung from IPF?

ANA

Bronchial biopsy

BAL

HRCT Thorax

Transfer factor

ANSWERS:

BAL (Bronchoalveolar lavage)

Correct Answer:

BAL (Bronchoalveolar lavage)

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

70-year-old man with 1 year of progressive breathlessness → chronic

interstitial lung disease

•

Worked on a farm for most of his life → strong exposure history to
organic

antigens (mouldy hay, thermophilic actinomycetes)

•

Widespread inspiratory crackles → interstitial lung pathology

•

Chest X-ray: diffuse alveolar shadowing → not specific; seen in both

hypersensitivity pneumonitis and IPF

The key diagnostic challenge here is Farmer's lung (chronic
hypersensitivity

pneumonitis) vs idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is the best investigation to differentiate
Farmer's

lung from IPF.

Why BAL is decisive:

•

Farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis):

o

BAL shows lymphocytosis (often \>30--40%)

o

Reflects immune-mediated alveolitis

•

IPF:

o

BAL shows neutrophil predominance

o

Lymphocytosis is absent or minimal

This difference directly reflects the pathophysiology:

•

Farmer's lung → immune hypersensitivity

reaction

•

IPF → fibrotic, non-inflammatory process

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• BAL lymphocytosis strongly favours hypersensitivity pneumonitis over
IPF.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

ANA

•

Used to screen for connective tissue disease--associated ILD

•

Does not differentiate Farmer's lung from IPF

Bronchial biopsy

•

Invasive

•

Rarely required to differentiate these two conditions

HRCT Thorax

•

Very useful for ILD characterization

•

However:

o

Overlap exists between chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis and IPF

o

Both may show fibrotic changes

•

HRCT supports but does not definitively differentiate

Transfer factor (DLCO):

•

Reduced in both Farmer's lung and IPF

•

Reflects disease severity, not aetiology

Key Points:

• BAL is the key investigation to distinguish Farmer's lung
(lymphocytosis)

from IPF (neutrophils).

stem: 60 year old with headache, jaw pain, and sudden visual symptoms. ESR 120. Diagnosis and eye complication?
explanation:
complication is

ischaemic optic neuropathy (ION).

Why ischaemic optic neuropathy occurs:

•

GCA causes granulomatous inflammation of medium and large arteries

•

Involvement of:

o

Posterior ciliary arteries

o

Branches of the ophthalmic artery

•

This leads to reduced blood supply to the optic nerve head

•

Result → Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION)

Clinical consequences:

Sudden, painless, often irreversible visual loss

•

Can progress rapidly to bilateral blindness if untreated

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Visual loss in giant cell arteritis is due to ischaemic optic
neuropathy---not

optic neuritis.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Anterior uveitis

•

Presents with:

o

Painful red eye

o

Photophobia

•

Associated with:

o

HLA-B27 diseases

o

Sarcoidosis

•

Not a complication of GCA

Optic neuritis

•

Typically affects young adults

•

Associated with:

o

Multiple sclerosis

•

Pain on eye movement

•

Inflammatory demyelination, not vascular

•

ESR/CRP usually normal

Key Points:

• In giant cell arteritis, visual loss occurs due to anterior ischaemic
optic

neuropathy from compromised posterior ciliary artery blood flow.

MOA of Rituximab

ANSWERS:

Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody causing B-cell

depletion

Correct Answer

Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody causing B-cell depletion

Key Points from the Question

•

Question asks mechanism of action (MOA) → classic MRCP pharmacology /

immunology SBA

•

Rituximab is widely tested across:

o

Rheumatology

o

Haematology

o

Nephrology

•

Understanding target antigen + downstream effect is essential

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody directed against CD20, a
surface

antigen expressed on B lymphocytes.

Mechanism of action (high-yield):

•

Binds to CD20 antigen on:

o

Pre-B cells

o

Mature B cells

•

Leads to B-cell depletion via:

o

Complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC)

o

Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC)

o

Apoptosis

Result:

•

↓ B-cell numbers

•

↓ Autoantibody production

↓ Immune-mediated tissue damage

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Plasma cells do NOT express CD20, so existing antibodies may persist
initially.

Where Rituximab Is Used:

Rheumatoid arthritis

•

ANCA-associated vasculitis

•

SLE (refractory cases)

•

ITP

•

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

•

Renal transplant rejection (antibody-mediated)

Common MRCP Traps (What Rituximab Does NOT Do):

•

Does not block TNF-α (that's infliximab, adalimumab)

•

Does not suppress T cells directly

•

Does not inhibit IL-6 (that's tocilizumab)

Key Points:

Rituximab works by targeting CD20 on B cells, causing B-cell depletion
and

reducing autoantibody-mediated disease.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of teriparatide?
options: Intermittent PTH analogue stimulating osteoblast bone formation
Inhibits RANKL to reduce osteoclast activity
Selectively blocks oestrogen receptors in bone
explanation:
osteoblast

activity and increases bone formation

Correct Answer

Intermittent parathyroid hormone (PTH) analogue that stimulates
osteoblast

activity and increases bone formation

Key Points from the Question

•

Asking for mechanism of action (MOA) → classic MRCP pharmacology

•

Teriparatide is used in severe osteoporosis

•

Exam trap often tests the difference between intermittent vs continuous

PTH exposure

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Teriparatide is a recombinant human parathyroid hormone (PTH 1--34).

Core mechanism:

•

When given intermittently (once daily subcutaneous injection):

o

Preferentially stimulates osteoblast activity

o

Increases bone formation

o

Improves bone mineral density

o

Reduces vertebral and non-vertebral fractures

Why intermittent dosing matters:

•

Continuous PTH exposure → ↑ osteoclast activity → bone resorption

•

Intermittent PTH exposure → ↑ osteoblast survival and function → net
bone

gain

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Teriparatide is the only osteoporosis drug that is primarily anabolic,
not

anti-resorptive.

Used in:

•

Severe osteoporosis

•

Multiple fragility fractures

•

Failure or intolerance of bisphosphonates

•

Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (high risk)

Contraindicated in:

•

Paget's disease

•

Bone malignancy

•

Prior skeletal radiotherapy

•

Hypercalcaemia

Common MRCP Traps

•

Not a bisphosphonate (those inhibit osteoclasts)

•

Not denosumab (RANKL inhibitor)

•

Continuous PTH would worsen osteoporosis

Key Concepts:

• Teriparatide is an anabolic osteoporosis drug: intermittent PTH
analogue

→ stimulates osteoblasts → increases bone formation.

stem: 68 year old had TIA despite aspirin; intolerant to clopidogrel. Dipyridamole added. Mechanism of dipyridamole?
options: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase (raises cAMP → inhibits platelet aggregation)
explanation:
phosphodiesterase (PDE) in platelets.

Mechanism (high-yield):

•

Inhibition of PDE → prevents breakdown of cyclic AMP (cAMP)

•

↑ cAMP within platelets → reduces platelet activation and aggregation

•

Also:

o

Inhibits adenosine uptake → ↑ extracellular adenosine → further ↑ cAMP

Net effect:

•

Antiplatelet action

•

Used in secondary prevention of TIA and ischaemic stroke, especially:

o

When aspirin alone is insufficient

o

When clopidogrel is contraindicated or not tolerated

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Dipyridamole works by increasing platelet cAMP via phosphodiesterase

inhibition.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Antagonizes ADP

•

This is the mechanism of:

o

Clopidogrel

o

Prasugrel

o

Ticagrelor

•

Dipyridamole does not block ADP receptors

C. Inhibition of cyclooxygenase

•

This is the mechanism of aspirin

•

Dipyridamole does not inhibit COX

D. Stimulation of AMP

•

Dipyridamole does not stimulate AMP production

•

It increases cAMP levels indirectly by preventing its breakdown

Key Points:

• Dipyridamole inhibits phosphodiesterase, increasing platelet cAMP and

reducing platelet aggregation---used in secondary stroke prevention.

MOA of Metformin

ANSWERS:

Activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) leading to reduced
hepatic

gluconeogenesis and increased insulin sensitivity

Correct Answer:

Activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) leading to reduced
hepatic

gluconeogenesis and increased insulin sensitivity

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Metformin is a biguanide that lowers blood glucose without increasing
insulin

secretion.

Core mechanisms (high-yield):

Activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase)

→ central metabolic "energy sensor"

↓ Hepatic gluconeogenesis

→ main glucose-lowering effect

↑ Peripheral insulin sensitivity (muscle, adipose tissue)

↓ Intestinal glucose absorption (minor

contribution)

What metformin does NOT do:

•

Does not stimulate pancreatic β-cells

•

Therefore, does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone

Metformin lowers glucose by suppressing liver glucose output, not by

increasing insulin.

Additional MRCP-Relevant Points:

•

Causes weight neutrality or weight loss

•

Improves lipid profile

•

Contraindicated in:

o

eGFR \<30 mL/min

o

Severe hepatic failure

o

Risk of lactic acidosis (rare but exam-relevant)

Key Points:

• Metformin activates AMPK → reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and

increases insulin sensitivity without causing hypoglycaemia.

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

78-year-old woman found collapsed → medical emergency

•

GCS 7 → severe CNS depression

Very high lithium level

Small molecule

Low protein binding

Water soluble

Renal impairment

urgent

Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes

Calcium channel blocker toxicity

Chelator for:

Iron

Aluminium

No role in lithium toxicity

Used for:

Methanol poisoning

Ethylene glycol poisoning

No effect on lithium

stem: A 22 year old female presents with lethargy, anorexia, weight loss, and peripheral neuropathy. Never on medication. Calcium 2.20 (low). What is the most likely cause of the low calcium?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

22-year-old woman with:

o

Lethargy, anorexia, weight loss → uraemic symptoms

o

Peripheral oedema → nephrotic / renal pathology

•

BP 163/83 mmHg → renal-related hypertension

•

Urine: protein 3+, blood 1+ → intrinsic renal disease (glomerular)

•

Creatinine 695 µmol/L → advanced chronic kidney disease

•

Calcium low (1.71 mmol/L)

•

Phosphate high (2.20 mmol/L)

This is a classic picture of advanced CKD with secondary metabolic bone
disease.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

In chronic kidney disease, hypocalcaemia occurs primarily due to reduced

gastrointestinal absorption of calcium.

Pathophysiology:

Diseased kidneys fail to convert:

o

25-hydroxyvitamin D → 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)

↓ Calcitriol leads to:

o

Reduced intestinal absorption of calcium

Concurrently:

o

Phosphate retention → binds calcium → worsens hypocalcaemia

Result:

Hypocalcaemia

o

Secondary hyperparathyroidism (not yet described but expected)

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Low calcium + high phosphate + very high creatinine = CKD-related

hypocalcaemia due to reduced vitamin D activation and reduced GI

calcium absorption.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Increased osteoblast activity

•

Would increase bone formation and potentially increase calcium uptake
into

bone

•

Not the primary mechanism in CKD-related hypocalcaemia

B. Increased urinary calcium loss

•

In advanced CKD, urinary calcium excretion is reduced, not increased

•

Hypocalcaemia is not due to renal calcium wasting

C. Parathyroid gland hypoplasia

•

Causes hypoparathyroidism

•

CKD causes secondary hyperparathyroidism, not hypoplasia

E. Reduced osteoblast sensitivity to PTH

•

PTH resistance is seen in pseudohypoparathyroidism

•

Not the mechanism in CKD-related hypocalcaemia

Key Points:

• In advanced CKD, hypocalcaemia occurs due to failure of renal vitamin
D

activation leading to reduced gastrointestinal calcium absorption.

stem: Achalasia — which intervention is most likely to definitively resolve symptoms?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Diagnosis implied: Achalasia

•

Achalasia is due to:

o

Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) relaxation

o

Loss of oesophageal peristalsis

•

Symptoms (classically tested, even if not restated here):

o

Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids

o

Regurgitation

o

Weight loss

o

Chest discomfort

•

Question asks which intervention will most likely

resolve symptoms → looking

for definitive therapy, not temporary relief

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Surgical cardiomyotomy (Heller myotomy) is the most effective and
definitive

treatment for achalasia.

Why cardiomyotomy works:

•

It divides the lower oesophageal sphincter muscle

•

Permanently reduces LOS pressure

•

Restores oesophageal emptying by gravity

•

Provides long-term symptom relief in the majority of patients

Key Points:

•

Gold standard definitive treatment

•

Often combined with partial fundoplication to reduce reflux

•

Superior durability compared to medical therapy

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Achalasia = mechanical outflow obstruction → best treated by

mechanically relieving the obstruction (myotomy).

Why Other Option Is Less Likely:

Calcium Channel Blockers (CCB):

•

Mechanism:

o

Reduce LOS pressure pharmacologically

•

Limitations:

o

Only modest, short-term benefit

o

Poor long-term efficacy

o

Side effects (hypotension, headache)

•

Reserved for:

o

Patients unfit for surgery

Temporary symptom relief

Not definitive and does not reliably resolve symptoms

Key Points:

• Achalasia symptoms are best resolved by surgical cardiomyotomy, not

medical therapy. Calcium channel blockers provide only temporary relief.

At the peak of the R wave
Between the P wave and QRS complex
At the start of the QRS complex
explanation:

Immediately after the T wave (end of ventricular repolarisation)

Key Points from the Question

•

Asking about isovolumetric (isovolumic) dilation / relaxation

•

Requires correlating mechanical cardiac events with the ECG

•

This is a classic MRCP physiology integration question

Detailed Explanation:

Isovolumetric relaxation (also called isovolumetric diastole) occurs:

•

After ventricular systole has ended

•

Before ventricular filling begins

Aortic and pulmonary valves have just closed

Mitral and tricuspid valves are still closed

•

Ventricular volume remains constant, but pressure is falling

ECG Correlation:

T wave = ventricular repolarisation

•

Semilunar valves close → S2

Isovolumetric relaxation begins

o

Ventricular pressure \< atrial pressure

AV valves open → ventricular filling starts

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Isovolumetric relaxation occurs after the T wave and before the next P

wave.

Key Notes:

• Isovolumetric dilation occurs immediately after the T wave on ECG.

stem: A 68 year old presented with 12 months H/O worsening symptoms of falling, which worsens with getting up from seated position & gaze palsy She has a shuffling gait, and her mother died from Huntington cornea. Her father suffered from idiopathic Parkinson\'s disease. What test will confirm her diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

68-year-old with 12 months of progressive falls → early falls are a red
flag

for atypical parkinsonism

•

Falls worse when rising from a seated position →

axial instability

•

Gaze palsy → particularly suggests supranuclear (vertical) gaze
involvement

•

Shuffling gait → parkinsonian feature

Family history:

o

Mother with Huntington's disease

o

Father with idiopathic Parkinson's disease

→ important distractors, but current phenotype does not fit either

The combination of early postural instability + gaze palsy is classic
for Progressive

Supranuclear Palsy (PSP).

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is an atypical parkinsonian
disorder (a

tauopathy).

Why MRI brain confirms the diagnosis:

•

MRI shows characteristic midbrain atrophy with:

o

Preserved pons

o

Resulting in the "hummingbird sign" or "penguin sign"

•

This imaging finding is highly supportive and exam-favourite for PSP

Clinical--radiological correlation:

•

Vertical gaze palsy → midbrain involvement

•

Early falls and axial rigidity → brainstem degeneration

•

Poor response to levodopa (often mentioned in other stems)

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Early falls + vertical gaze palsy = PSP → confirm with MRI brain
(midbrain

atrophy).

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Autonomic testing

•

Useful for multiple system atrophy (MSA)

PSP does not primarily cause early autonomic failure

B. DATscan

•

Shows reduced dopaminergic uptake

•

Abnormal in:

o

Parkinson's disease

o

PSP

o

MSA

•

Cannot differentiate PSP from idiopathic Parkinson's disease

D. Genetic testing

•

Relevant for:

o

Huntington's disease

o

Some familial parkinsonian syndromes

•

PSP is sporadic, not genetically confirmed in routine practice

Key points:

• Progressive supranuclear palsy is confirmed with MRI brain showing

midbrain atrophy (hummingbird sign), not DATscan or genetic testing.

stem: Male with 1-week worsening rash. Brief URTI 1 week ago. Herald patch noted. Pityriasis rosea diagnosed. Causative agent?
explanation:

•

Male with 1-week history of worsening rash

•

Preceded by a brief URTI → viral prodrome

•

Clinical diagnosis: pityriasis rosea

•

Acute onset, self-limiting papulosquamous eruption

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Pityriasis rosea is strongly associated with reactivation of human
herpesviruses,

particularly:

•

HHV-7 (most strongly linked)

•

HHV-6 (also implicated, but less commonly tested)

Why HHV-7 is the best answer:

•

Evidence supports viral reactivation, not primary infection

•

Explains:

o

Preceding upper respiratory tract symptoms

o

Sudden onset of rash

•

Produces the classic sequence:

o

Herald patch

o

Followed by generalised rash in a "Christmas tree" distribution

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

Pityriasis rosea = HHV-7 reactivation

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

HSV

•

Causes vesicular lesions (oral/genital herpes)

•

Not associated with pityriasis rosea

Malassezia

•

Causes pityriasis versicolor

•

Hypo/hyperpigmented scaly patches

•

No viral prodrome

Trichophyton rubrum

•

Dermatophyte → tinea infections

•

Ring-shaped, itchy lesions

•

Chronic fungal infection, not acute viral rash

Varicella

•

Causes chickenpox

•

Vesicular rash in different stages

•

Systemic illness more severe

Key Points:

• Pityriasis rosea is most commonly associated with HHV-7 reactivation,

50 years female presented with painful lumps on legs & fatigue. No PMH.
Only

medication is OCP.

Diagnosis?

Cutaneous sarcoidosis

Erythema nodosum

Lichen plants

Psoriasis

ANSWERS:

Erythema nodosum

Correct Answer:

Erythema nodosum

Key Points from the Scenario

•

50-year-old female

•

Painful lumps on legs → key descriptive clue

•

Fatigue → systemic inflammatory feature

•

No past medical history

•

Only medication: oral contraceptive pill (OCP) → recognised trigger

The combination of painful nodules on the legs + systemic symptoms is
highly

characteristic.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Erythema nodosum (EN) is an inflammatory panniculitis affecting the

subcutaneous fat, classically presenting with:

•

Tender, painful, erythematous nodules

•

Typically, on the anterior shins

•

Associated with systemic symptoms (fatigue, malaise, arthralgia)

Why EN fits perfectly here:

•

Painful lesions → distinguishes EN from many dermatoses

•

Leg involvement → classic site

•

OCP use → well-known precipitating factor

•

Often occurs without prior systemic disease

Common associations:

•

OCP / pregnancy

•

Sarcoidosis

•

Streptococcal infection

•

TB

•

IBD

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Painful nodules on the shins = erythema nodosum until proven
otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Cutaneous sarcoidosis

•

Usually non-tender

•

May present as plaques, papules, lupus pernio

•

Erythema nodosum can be associated with sarcoidosis, but the primary

Lichen planus

•

Intensely itchy

•

Violaceous, flat-topped papules

•

stem: Man with rash, malaise and lethargy. His young son had a fever and facial rash recently. Bloods: Hb 70s MCV 80, WCC normal, Platelets normal. B/M showed red cell aplasia. What's the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

Man with rash, malaise, lethargy → viral prodrome

•

Recent exposure: young son with fever and facial rash → classic slapped-

cheek illness

•

Bloods:

o

Hb in the 70s → severe anaemia

o

MCV 80 (normocytic) → not iron deficiency

o

WCC normal, platelets normal → isolated red cell problem

•

Bone marrow: red cell aplasia → selective suppression of erythropoiesis

The defining clues are child with facial rash + isolated severe
anaemia + red cell

aplasia.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Parvovirus B19 selectively infects and destroys erythroid precursor
cells in the bone

marrow.

Pathophysiology:

•

Virus binds to P antigen on erythroid progenitors

•

Causes transient arrest of red cell production

•

Results in:

o

Pure red cell aplasia

o

Severe anaemia

o

Normal white cells and platelets

Clinical settings where this is seen:

•

Adults exposed to children with erythema infectiosum

•

Patients with underlying haemolytic anaemia (aplastic crisis)

•

Immunocompromised patients (chronic PRCA)

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Isolated anaemia with red cell aplasia following

exposure to a child with

"slapped-cheek" rash = Parvovirus B19.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

CMV

•

Causes:

o

Systemic illness

o

Cytopenias (often leukopenia, thrombocytopenia)

•

Does not cause isolated red cell aplasia

EBV

•

Causes:

o

Infectious mononucleosis

o

Lymphocytosis, atypical lymphocytes

•

Bone marrow not selectively suppressed

Rubella

•

Causes mild viral illness with rash

•

Does not cause pure red cell aplasia

•

Mainly important in pregnancy (congenital rubella)

Toxoplasmosis

•

Causes:

o

Lymphadenopathy

o

CNS disease in immunocompromised

•

No association with red cell aplasia

Key Points:

• Parvovirus B19 causes pure red cell aplasia and

severe normocytic

anaemia after exposure to a child with erythema infectiosum.

Acute onset rash

No mention of:

Sexual risk factors

Mucosal lesions

Systemic features of syphilis
