stem: Middle-aged lady with hypercholesterolaemia and SVT/asthma on beclomethasone. Started on a statin. Simvastatin level unexpectedly high. Drug interaction mechanism?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Middle-aged woman with hypercholesterolaemia

•

History of SVT → likely on diltiazem

•

Asthma → beta-blockers avoided (context, not core to interaction)

•

Atorvastatin prescribed for lipid control

•

Question asks for mechanism of interaction, not clinical consequence

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker and a
moderate

inhibitor of CYP3A4.

Atorvastatin is predominantly metabolised by CYP3A4.

What happens when they are combined:

•

Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4

•

↓ Metabolism of atorvastatin

•

↑ Plasma concentration and bioavailability of atorvastatin

•

↑ Risk of:

o

Myopathy

o

Rhabdomyolysis (dose-related risk)

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Diltiazem + atorvastatin → CYP3A4 inhibition → increased statin
levels.

(Same principle applies to verapamil, erythromycin, clarithromycin,
azoles, grapefruit

juice.)

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

Increase availability

•

This is an effect, not a mechanism

Decrease renal clearance

•

Atorvastatin is not primarily renally excreted

•

Renal clearance interactions are relevant for drugs like:

o

Digoxin

o

Lithium

Key Points:

• Diltiazem increases atorvastatin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4
metabolism

--- always think cytochrome P450 interactions when combining these

drugs.

stem: Young patient presents with recurrent renal calculi & on U/R/E Hematuria pH = low Na+ 140 K+ 2.7 Urinary pH = low Where is the defect?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Young patient with recurrent renal calculi

•

Haematuria → stone-related mucosal irritation

•

Serum potassium low (K⁺ = 2.7 mmol/L) → hypokalaemia

•

Urinary pH = low (acidic urine) → kidneys are still able to acidify
urine

•

Electrolytes otherwise unremarkable

The two decisive clues are:

•

Hypokalaemia

•

Low urinary pH (ability to acidify urine preserved)

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

This presentation is most consistent with proximal renal tubular
acidosis (Type 2

RTA), where the defect lies in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT).

Pathophysiology:

•

The PCT normally reabsorbs \~85--90% of filtered bicarbonate

•

In proximal RTA:

o

Impaired bicarbonate reabsorption → bicarbonate wasting

o

Plasma bicarbonate falls

•

Once plasma bicarbonate drops below the renal threshold:

The distal nephron can still acidify urine

o

Hence urinary pH becomes low (\<5.5)

Why stones occur:

•

Chronic bicarbonate loss → metabolic acidosis

•

Acidosis promotes:

o

Bone buffering

o

Hypercalciuria

•

This predisposes to renal calculi

•

Hypokalaemia is typical due to increased distal sodium delivery →
potassium

loss

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

Low urinary pH + hypokalaemia + renal stones = proximal (Type 2) RTA →
PCT

defect.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

DCT (Distal convoluted tubule):

•

Distal RTA (Type 1) defect

•

Characterised by:

o

Inability to acidify urine

o

High urine pH (\>5.5)

o

Nephrocalcinosis

•

This patient has low urine pH

Loop of Henle

•

Loop defects cause:

o

Salt wasting

o

Bartter syndrome--like picture

•

Not associated with RTA or acidic urine

Collecting duct

•

Type 1 (distal) or Type 4 RTA

•

Type 4 RTA causes hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia

Key Points:

• Proximal RTA (PCT defect) presents with hypokalaemia and low urinary

pH, and can be associated with recurrent renal stones.

ALTERNATIVE OPINION

Young patient presents with recurrent renal calculi & on U/R/E Hematuria

Potassium 2.9

Bicarbonate 10

Creatinine 103

Urinary pH 6.4

Urine amino acid screen negative

Where is the defect?

DCT

PCT

Loop of Henle

Collecting duct

ANSWERS:

Collecting duct

Correct Answer

Collecting duct

Key Points from the Scenario

•

Young patient + recurrent renal calculi + haematuria → think renal
tubular

acidosis (RTA), especially the type associated with stones

•

K⁺ 2.9 (low) → hypokalaemia (seen in Type 1 and Type 2 RTA)

•

HCO₃⁻ 10 (very low) → significant metabolic acidosis

•

Creatinine 103 → renal function essentially preserved (so this is not
just

"uraemic acidosis")

•

Urinary pH 6.4 → inappropriately high in the

presence of metabolic acidosis

(kidneys should be making urine acidic, \<5.5)

•

Urine amino acid screen negative → argues against Fanconi syndrome /

proximal tubule defect

The key discriminator is metabolic acidosis + urine pH persistently
\>5.5.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

This is Distal (Type 1) Renal Tubular Acidosis, due to failure of acid
secretion by α-

intercalated cells in the collecting duct.

Pathophysiology:

•

Collecting duct normally secretes H⁺ → acidifies urine

•

In Type 1 (distal) RTA:

o

Cannot excrete H⁺

o

Urine stays alkaline (pH \>5.5) despite systemic acidosis

o

Leads to:

▪

Hypokalaemia

▪

Calcium phosphate stones / nephrocalcinosis (because alkaline

urine promotes stone formation)

What happens in Distal (Type 1) RTA

Feature Explanation

Urine pH high (\>5.5) Cannot secrete H⁺

Metabolic acidosis Acid retained

Hypokalaemia H⁺/K⁺ exchange impaired

Renal stones Alkaline urine → calcium phosphate stones

Normal renal function Tubular, not glomerular

This exact combination is CLASSIC for distal

(Type 1) RTA.

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Recurrent renal stones + metabolic acidosis + urine pH \>5.5 = distal
(Type

RTA → collecting duct defect.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

PCT (Proximal tubule)

•

Proximal (Type 2) RTA typically has:

o

Urine pH can fall to \<5.5 once plasma bicarbonate is low (distal

acidification intact)

o

Often associated with Fanconi features (glucosuria, aminoaciduria,

phosphaturia)

•

Here: urine pH is high (6.4) and amino acid

screen negative

DCT

•

The classic "can't acidify urine" RTA is distal/collecting duct, not
DCT in SBA

framing

Loop of Henle

•

Loop defects → Bartter-type salt wasting, not RTA with alkaline urine
and stones

Key Points:

This is Type 1 (distal) RTA: alkaline urine + hypokalaemic metabolic

acidosis + stones → collecting duct (α-intercalated cell) defect.

stem: A new test for cervical cancer. 50 patients with confirmed cancer were tested 47 tested positive and 3 tested negative. Calculate the sensitivity?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

50 patients with confirmed cervical cancer → this is the diseased
population

•

Test results:

o

47 tested positive → True Positives (TP)

o

3 tested negative → False Negatives (FN)

•

Question asks for sensitivity → ability of a test to correctly identify
those with

disease

Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN).

Here, 47 ÷ 50 = 94%.

stem: MOA of Lorazepam?
explanation:
•

It binds to the GABA_A receptor

•

Increases the frequency of chloride channel opening

•

Enhances the inhibitory effect of GABA in the CNS

•

Results in:

o

Anxiolysis

o

Sedation

o

Muscle relaxation

Anticonvulsant effect

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Benzodiazepines do not activate GABA directly; they potentiate GABA's

inhibitory action at the GABA_A receptor.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

A. Dopamine agonist

•

Mechanism of drugs like pramipexole, bromocriptine

Not related to benzodiazepines

C. Serotonin inhibitor

stem: Female with 6 months loose stool, abdominal bloating, MCV 97, low Hb, and history of excess alcohol. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

6 months history of loose stools and abdominal bloating → chronic

malabsorption picture

•

Macrocytosis (MCV 97) → suggests folate deficiency (or early B12
deficiency)

•

Low haemoglobin → anaemia due to malabsorption

•

History of alcohol overdose → important red herring, but does not
explain

chronic diarrhoea + bloating

•

No mention of:

o

Fever

o

Arthralgia

o

Neurological features (which would suggest Whipple's)

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Coeliac disease is a chronic immune-mediated enteropathy caused by
gluten

sensitivity, leading to small intestinal villous atrophy.

Why coeliac disease fits best:

•

Causes chronic diarrhoea and abdominal bloating

•

Leads to malabsorption of nutrients, especially:

o

Folate → macrocytosis (↑ MCV)

Iron → anaemia (often mixed picture)

•

Symptoms may be subtle and prolonged over months

•

Commonly presents in adult females with non-specific GI symptoms

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Chronic diarrhoea + bloating + macrocytic anaemia = coeliac disease
until

proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

A. Alcohol overdose

•

Causes:

o

Acute gastritis

o

Acute metabolic derangements

•

Does not cause chronic diarrhoea and bloating

•

Macrocytosis from alcohol occurs due to marrow toxicity, but does not
explain

malabsorptive GI symptoms

C. Whipple's disease

•

Rare

•

Usually presents with:

o

Weight loss

o

Diarrhoea

o

Arthralgia

o

Neurological or cardiac features

•

Typically affects middle-aged men

•

Not the most likely first diagnosis in this context

Key Concepts:

• Chronic diarrhoea, bloating, and macrocytic anaemia strongly suggest

coeliac disease --- even in the presence of alcohol history.

BMI with height relation, how to represent?

A. Histogram

B. Scatter line

C. Pie chart

ANSWERS:

Scatter plot (scatter diagram)

Correct Answer:

B. Scatter plot (scatter diagram)

Key Points from the Question:

•

Variables involved:

o

BMI → continuous numerical variable

o

Height → continuous numerical variable

•

The aim is to show the relationship / correlation between two continuous

variables

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

A scatter plot is the correct way to represent the relationship between
two

Why scatter plot is best:

•

Each point represents one individual

•

Allows assessment of:

o

Direction of relationship (positive / negative)

Strength of correlation

o

Outliers

Can add:

o

Line of best fit (regression line) if needed

• Relationship between two continuous variables → Scatter plot.

Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:

A. Histogram

Used for distribution of a single continuous variable

•

Cannot show relationship between two variables

C. Pie chart

Not suitable for continuous variables or relationships

correlation between two continuous variables.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of dabigatran?
explanation:
Key Points from the Question:

•

Asking for mechanism of action (MOA) → classic MRCP pharmacology

•

Dabigatran is one of the DOACs

•

Important to distinguish:

o

Thrombin inhibitors vs Factor Xa inhibitors

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Dabigatran is a direct, competitive inhibitor of thrombin (Factor IIa).

How it works:

•

Thrombin (Factor IIa) normally:

o

Converts fibrinogen → fibrin

o

Activates factors V, VIII, XI

o

Activates platelets

•

Dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin, leading to:

o

↓ fibrin formation

o

↓ clot propagation

o

↓ platelet activation

Acts on free thrombin and clot-bound thrombin

Does not require antithrombin III

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

• Dabigatran is the only commonly used oral direct thrombin inhibitor

Relevant Points:

•

Given as dabigatran etexilate (prodrug)

•

Mainly renally excreted

•

Antidote: Idarucizumab

•

Prolongs aPTT (useful exam clue)

Key Points:

• Dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin (Factor IIa), preventing fibrin

formation and clot development.

stem: A 35 y/o female in genetic clinic. Brother and son have Becker's muscular dystrophy. What is her risk of being carrier?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

Becker's muscular dystrophy (BMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder

•

Affected individuals:

o

Brother → confirms the mutation is present in her family

o

Son → proves she has already transmitted the affected X chromosome

•

The patient herself is female → can be a carrier, not affected

The presence of an affected son is the single most important clue.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Becker's muscular dystrophy follows X-linked recessive inheritance.

What does an affected son imply?

•

A male child inherits:

o

Y chromosome from father

o

X chromosome from mother

•

Therefore, if her son has Becker's MD, the mutant X must have come from

her

So:

•

She is definitely carrying one affected X chromosome

•

Females have two X chromosomes

o

One affected

o

One normal

Hence, she is a heterozygous carrier.

Carrier status probability:

•

1 affected X out of 2 X chromosomes

•

= 50% carrier

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Any woman with an affected son with an X-linked recessive condition is
an

obligate carrier (50%).

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

•

0%

→ Impossible --- her son is affected

•

25%

→ Applies to future offspring risk, not her carrier status

•

75%

→ Not a valid probability in X-linked inheritance

•

100%

→ Would imply both X chromosomes are affected

(she would be symptomatic,

which she is not)

Key Points:

• A woman with an affected son from an X-linked recessive disorder has a

50% chance of being a carrier --- in fact, she is an obligate carrier.

stem: A 22 y/o female, right sided motor seizure, progressives to generalisation. Has area of deep red discolouration, extending over left forehead since childhood. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

22-year-old female

•

Focal (right-sided) motor seizure progressing to generalisation →
suggests

a structural cortical lesion

•

Deep red discolouration over the left forehead since childhood → classic

port-wine stain

•

Lesion is congenital and unilateral, involving the trigeminal (V1)
distribution

The combination of facial port-wine stain + seizures is the critical
diagnostic clue.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Sturge--Weber syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder
characterised by:

•

Facial capillary malformation (port-wine stain)

o

Typically in ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal distribution

•

Leptomeningeal angiomas on the ipsilateral cerebral cortex

•

These vascular malformations cause:

o

Focal seizures (often starting in childhood)

o

Contralateral motor symptoms

o

Possible progressive neurological deficits

Why this fits perfectly:

•

Congenital deep red facial lesion → port-wine stain

•

Seizures starting focally → cortical irritation from leptomeningeal
angioma

•

Later generalisation → common seizure evolution in Sturge--Weber

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Port-wine stain in V1 distribution + seizures = Sturge--Weber syndrome

until proven otherwise.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

AV malformation

•

Can cause focal seizures

•

Does NOT cause congenital facial port-wine stain

Neurofibromatosis (NF)

•

Features:

o

Café-au-lait spots

o

Neurofibromas

o

Optic gliomas

•

Port-wine stain is not a feature

Tuberous sclerosis (TS)

•

Features:

o

Facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum)

o

Hypomelanotic "ash-leaf" spots

o

Cortical tubers

•

Lesions are not port-wine stains

Key Points:

• Congenital port-wine stain over the face with focal seizures strongly

indicates Sturge--Weber syndrome.

stem: A baby is born with a congenital heart defect. The mother is anti-Ro antibody positive. What cardiac defect is most likely in the neonate?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Congenital defect

•

Presence of anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies

•

This immediately points to maternal autoantibody--mediated fetal cardiac

involvement

Anti-Ro antibodies are classically associated with neonatal lupus, the
most serious

cardiac manifestation being congenital heart block.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies can cross the placenta from mother to fetus.

Pathophysiology:

•

Maternal anti-Ro antibodies bind to fetal cardiac conduction tissue

•

Cause immune-mediated inflammation and fibrosis of:

o

AV node

o

His--Purkinje system

•

This leads to irreversible congenital complete heart block (3rd-degree
AV

block)

Key clinical facts:

•

Occurs in infants of mothers with:

o

SLE

o

Sjögren's syndrome

o

Or asymptomatic anti-Ro positivity

•

Fetal bradycardia may be detected antenatally

•

Many infants require permanent pacemaker

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Anti-Ro antibody → neonatal lupus → congenital complete heart block.

Important Exclusions

•

Not associated with:

o

Structural septal defects

o

Valvular disease

o

Cardiomyopathy

•

This is a conduction abnormality, not an anatomical defect

Key Points:

• Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies cause immune-mediated damage to the fetal AV

node, resulting in congenital complete heart block.

stem: A middle-aged person had H/O swelling and pain in his great toe earlier, now presented with pain and swelling in the knee. What will you find in synovial fluid?
Osteogenesis Imperfecta scenario (H/O recurrent fractures since childhood with family history). Defective protein?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Recurrent fractures since childhood → suggests a congenital bone
fragility

disorder

•

Positive family history → inherited condition

•

Typical MRCP stem for osteogenesis imperfecta (OI)

•

Question asks specifically for the defective protein

The combination of early-onset fractures + inheritance is classic for
OI.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

Osteogenesis imperfecta is caused by a defect in Type I collagen, the
major

structural protein of bone.

Pathophysiology:

•

Mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes

•

Leads to:

o

↓ quantity or abnormal quality of Type I collagen

•

Type I collagen is a key component of:

o

Bone

o

Tendons

o

Sclera

o

Dentin

Clinical consequences:

•

Fragile bones → recurrent fractures

•

Blue sclera

•

Hearing loss

•

Dentinogenesis imperfecta (in some types)

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• OI = Type I collagen defect → brittle bones from childhood.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Fibrillin

•

Defective in Marfan syndrome

•

Causes:

o

Tall stature

Aortic root dilation

o

Lens dislocation

Elastin

•

Involved in elastic tissue disorders

•

Associated with:

o

Cutis laxa

o

Supravalvular aortic stenosis

Osteopontin

•

Bone matrix protein

•

Not implicated in inherited brittle bone disease

Key Points:

• Osteogenesis imperfecta is caused by a defect in Type I collagen.

stem: Which of the following is a TRUE contraindication to penicillin use?
options: Blistering rash in mouth and body 5 days after starting antibiotics (Stevens-Johnson syndrome — true allergy)
Morbilliform rash 2 days after starting penicillin (likely viral — not true allergy)
Mother had penicillin allergy (family history alone is not a contraindication)
Mild urticaria resolving after stopping penicillin
explanation:
Blistering rash involving mouth and body 5 days after starting
antibiotics

Key Points from the Scenario:

The question is asking when non-penicillin antibiotics are indicated,
i.e. true

penicillin allergy where penicillin must be avoided.

Detailed Explanation:

Blistering rash in mouth and body 5 days after starting antibiotics

•

Suggests severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction (SCAR):

o

Stevens--Johnson syndrome (SJS)

o

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)

•

Features:

o

Mucosal involvement

o

Blistering / epidermal detachment

o

Delayed onset (days)

•

This is a Type IV (T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity

•

Penicillin and all β-lactams are absolutely contraindicated lifelong

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

• Blistering + mucosal involvement = SJS/TEN → absolute contraindication

to penicillin.

Why the Other Options Are NOT Indications

Morbilliform rash 2 days after starting penicillin

Not an indication

•

This is the commonest benign drug rash

•

Characteristics:

o

Maculopapular

o

No mucosal involvement

No blistering

•

Usually, non-IgE mediated

•

Penicillin can often be:

o

Re-used cautiously

o

Or switched within β-lactams if needed

CLUE:

• Morbilliform rash ≠ true penicillin allergy

Mother had penicillin allergy

Not an indication

•

Penicillin allergy is not inherited

•

Family history does not predict patient allergy

•

No restriction on penicillin use

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

•

Only severe delayed hypersensitivity reactions (e.g. SJS/TEN with
blistering

and mucosal involvement) mandate lifelong avoidance of penicillin and

use of non-penicillin antibiotics.

stem: Which area is targeted for ablation in atrial flutter?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario:

•

Question refers to atrial flutter, not atrial fibrillation

•

Asking specifically about the target for catheter ablation

•

MRCP commonly tests the re-entrant circuit anatomy of arrhythmias

Typical (common) atrial flutter has a well-defined macro--re-entrant
circuit.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Typical atrial flutter is caused by a macro--re-entrant circuit in the
right atrium.

The critical part of this circuit is the:

•

Cavotricuspid isthmus

o

The area of tissue between the tricuspid valve and the inferior vena

cava

Why ablation here works:

•

This is the slow-conduction zone essential for maintaining the flutter
circuit

•

Radiofrequency ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus interrupts the
circuit

•

Results in:

o

Very high success rates (\>90%)

o

Low recurrence

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

•

Typical atrial flutter = right atrial macro--re-entry → ablate the

cavotricuspid isthmus.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

AV node

•

AV node ablation:

o

Used for rate control, not rhythm cure

o

Leaves patient in permanent atrial flutter/fibrillation

o

Requires pacemaker

Pulmonary veins

•

Pulmonary vein isolation is the ablation target in atrial fibrillation

•

Not involved in atrial flutter re-entry circuit

Key Points:

•

Catheter ablation for typical atrial flutter targets the cavotricuspid

isthmus.

stem: Right Horner's syndrome, right gag reflex absent, right facial weaknesses Left deviation of tongue Slurring and dysphagia, tongue fasciculation Where is the lesion?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario (Localisation Clues):

Let's break the signs systematically:

•

Right Horner's syndrome

→ Disruption of descending sympathetic fibres (brainstem or cervico-

medullary region)

•

Right gag reflex absent + dysphagia + slurring

→ CN IX & X (nucleus ambiguus) involvement

→ Localises to the medulla

•

Tongue fasciculation + deviation

→ Lower motor neuron hypoglossal (CN XII) lesion

→ CN XII nucleus/nerve lies in the medulla

•

Combination of IX, X, XII involvement + Horner's

→ Points strongly to a medullary / cervico-medullary lesion

This constellation cannot be explained by a single supratentorial or
pontine lesion.

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer:

A cervico-medullary lesion (lower brainstem at the medulla--upper
cervical junction)

can involve:

•

Descending sympathetic fibres → Horner's syndrome

•

Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX & X) → dysphagia, absent gag reflex

•

Hypoglossal nucleus / nerve (CN XII) → tongue fasciculation and
deviation

This pattern is classically seen in medullary lesions (e.g. lateral or
extended medullary

syndromes, cervico-medullary compression).

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

•

Horner's syndrome + nucleus ambiguus signs + hypoglossal LMN features

= medullary / cervico-medullary lesion

Why Other Options Are Less Likely:

Cerebellopontine angle

•

Affects CN VII & VIII

•

Does not involve CN IX, X, XII or sympathetic fibres

Jugular foramen

•

Involves CN IX, X, XI

•

Does not affect CN XII

•

Horner's syndrome is not a consistent feature

Midbrain

•

Would cause:

o

Oculomotor palsy

o

Altered consciousness

•

No involvement of IX, X, XII

Pons

•

Facial nerve nucleus located here

•

Hypoglossal nucleus is not in the pons

•

Horner's + IX/X findings cannot be explained

Key Points:

•

Multiple lower cranial nerve palsies (IX, X, XII) with Horner's syndrome

localise the lesion to the cervico-medullary region.

stem: A 40 years old with previous H/O acute hepatitis C 6 months back. What to check for chronic hepatitis C?
explanation:
Correct Answer

HCV RNA PCR

Key Points from the Scenario:

•

40-year-old with acute hepatitis C 6 months ago

•

Question asks how to check for chronic hepatitis C

•

Time frame is crucial:

o

6 months after acute infection → now assessing persistence of virus

•

Chronic hepatitis C is defined by ongoing viral replication, not
antibody

presence

Detailed Explanation of the Correct Answer

Chronic hepatitis C is diagnosed by the presence of detectable HCV RNA
in blood

for \>6 months.

Why HCV RNA PCR is the correct test:

•

Detects active viral replication

•

Confirms whether the virus has:

o

Cleared spontaneously

o

OR progressed to chronic infection

•

Gold standard for:

o

Diagnosis of chronic HCV

o

Monitoring treatment response

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

•

Chronic HCV = persistent HCV RNA positivity at 6 months.

Why Other Options Are Less Appropriate:

Anti-HCV antibody

•

Indicates previous exposure only

•

Remains positive even after viral clearance

•

Cannot distinguish:

o

Past infection

o

Chronic active infection

Liver biopsy

•

Used to assess:

o

Degree of inflammation

o

Fibrosis

•

Not required to diagnose chronic HCV

Elastography

•

Assesses liver fibrosis

•

Useful after diagnosis, not for confirming chronic infection

Key Points:

•

To confirm chronic hepatitis C, always check HCV RNA PCR --- antibodies

alone are insufficient.

stem: What is the most common genetic mechanism responsible for trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)?
explanation:
Key Points from the Question:

•

Trisomy 21 = Down syndrome

•

Question asks for the genetic mechanism / mutation

•

MRCP commonly tests mechanism, not just association

Detailed Explanation:

The most common cause of trisomy 21 is meiotic

nondisjunction

What happens:

•

Failure of chromosome 21 to separate properly during meiosis

•

Results in a gamete with two copies of chromosome 21

•

After fertilisation → three copies of chromosome 21

When it occurs:

•

Usually during maternal meiosis I (most common)

•

Risk increases with advanced maternal age

MRCP Syndrome Pearl:

•

\~95% of Down syndrome cases are due to

meiotic nondisjunction.

Other (Less Common) Mechanisms

•

Robertsonian translocation (\~4%)

o

Often involving chromosomes 14 and 21

o

Important in recurrent Down syndrome

•

Mosaicism (\~1%)

o

Post-zygotic nondisjunction

o

Milder phenotype

Key Points:

•

Trisomy 21 is most commonly caused by meiotic nondisjunction, usually

during maternal meiosis I.

stem: Mechanism of PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)?
explanation:
Key Points from the Question:

•

PCR = Polymerase Chain Reaction

•

It is a molecular biology technique

•

Question is testing the core purpose, not individual steps

Detailed Explanation:

PCR is used to amplify a specific DNA sequence exponentially.

What PCR does:

•

Takes a small amount of DNA

•

Produces millions of copies of a target DNA segment

Core steps:

Denaturation -- DNA strands separate

Annealing -- primers bind to target DNA

Extension -- DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA

Requires DNA polymerase (e.g. Taq polymerase)

End result = DNA → more DNA

MRCP Syndrome pearl:

•

PCR amplifies DNA; it does not convert DNA to RNA or RNA to DNA.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

•

DNA → RNA

→ This is transcription, not PCR

•

RNA → DNA

→ This is reverse transcription (RT), used in RT-PCR, not standard PCR

Key Points:

•

PCR is a technique for DNA amplification --- producing millions of
copies

of a target DNA sequence.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of lorazepam?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Enhances GABA-A receptor--mediated inhibitory neurotransmission

Key Points

•

Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine

•

Acts on the GABA-A receptor in the CNS

•

Produces anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, and muscle-relaxant
effects

Detailed Explanation:

Lorazepam binds to the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor and:

•

Increases the frequency of chloride (Cl⁻) channel opening

Enhances the inhibitory effect of GABA

•

Leads to neuronal hyperpolarisation and reduced neuronal firing

Important exam nuance: Benzodiazepines do NOT activate GABA
directly---they

potentiate GABA's effect.

MRCP Syndrome Pearls:

•

Benzodiazepines → ↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening

•

Barbiturates → ↑ duration of Cl⁻ channel opening

•

Lorazepam is preferred in:

o

Acute anxiety

o

Status epilepticus

o

Alcohol withdrawal (less hepatic metabolism)

Key Points:

Lorazepam enhances GABA-A receptor activity by increasing chloride
channel

opening frequency, leading to CNS inhibition.

stem: 68 y/o. Presents 6wks fever, LOW, change in bowel habits. Pansystolic murmur to axillary. RIF Mass. Hb Low. MCV low. S. Bovis in culture. Aetiology?
explanation:
Correct Answer

Caecal carcinoma

Commonly caecal or proximal colon tumors.

stem: A 30 y/o presented with 2 weeks after head trauma with loss of consciousness upon which CT brain was done and was free. His family members reported taking thyroxine TSH = High T3 + T3 = Low Dx?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

•

30 y/o, head trauma -- CT brain free, excludes major pituitary
structural lesion.

•

On thyroxine (per family report) -- implies previous thyroid disease.

•

TSH = High, T3 & T4 = Low → Primary hypothyroidism pattern (thyroid

gland failure, not pituitary).

•

Hashimoto thyroiditis = most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in

young adults.

•

Pendred syndrome → congenital deafness + goitre, not suggested here.

•

Secondary hypothyroidism would show low/normal TSH with low T3/T4,

not high TSH.

Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disease where antibodies
destroy

the thyroid follicles, leading to decreased thyroid hormone production.

•

Lab hallmark: ↑TSH + ↓T3/T4 (primary hypothyroidism).

•

Patient already on thyroxine → indicates known thyroid disease.

•

Post-head trauma is a red herring here; thyroid profile confirms the
diagnosis.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Pendred syndrome → Presents with congenital sensorineural deafness +

goitre due to iodide organification defect. Not relevant here, no
deafness

history.

•

Secondary hypothyroidism → Would have low/normal TSH + low T3/T4,

due to pituitary or hypothalamic disease. This patient has high TSH,
so it's

primary, not secondary.

Final Diagnosis: Hashimoto thyroiditis (Primary Hypothyroidism)

High TSH, low FT3, FT4

Dx?

Hashimoto thyroiditis

stem: Newly admitted patient to ward with severe diarrhoea same day 4 of the inpatients also got affected with the same symptoms and one of the staff members sent home after getting sick. Aetiology?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

•

Newly admitted patient + 4 inpatients + 1 staff member → outbreak

pattern, highly infectious.

•

Severe diarrhoea, rapid onset → fits viral gastroenteritis.

Norovirus = most common cause of acute gastroenteritis outbreaks in

hospitals, cruise ships, nursing homes.

•

Rotavirus → mainly affects children, not adults in hospital outbreaks.

•

Campylobacter → foodborne, sporadic cases, not rapid hospital outbreak.

•

Giardia → causes prolonged watery diarrhoea, not sudden ward outbreak.

Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer

Norovirus is a highly contagious calicivirus spread via the faeco-oral
route and

contaminated surfaces.

•

Incubation: 24--48 hrs.

•

Symptoms: sudden onset diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, fever

sometimes.

•

Epidemiology: notorious for hospital and institutional outbreaks, staff
and

patients affected simultaneously.

•

Management: supportive, strict infection control, isolation of cases.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

Rotavirus → common in infants and children, not typical for adult
hospital

ward outbreak.

•

Campylobacter → foodborne, usually isolated case or family cluster, not

cross-infectious outbreak across ward + staff.

•

Giardia → causes chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption, bloating, not acute

explosive outbreak affecting many at once.

stem: Patient presented with paracetamol overdose today Which of the following is most likely not elevated at present?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

•

Paracetamol overdose -- today → very early presentation (within hours).

•

Liver damage timeline:

o

First 24h: patient may be asymptomatic or just nausea/vomiting.

o

24--72h: hepatocellular necrosis begins → ↑AST/ALT, ↑PT/INR.

o

Later (72--96h): jaundice develops → ↑bilirubin.

•

Cholestatic enzymes (ALP, GGT) and albumin don't change acutely; albumin

falls only in chronic disease.

Detailed Explanation of Correct Answer

•

In early paracetamol toxicity, the most sensitive indicators of
hepatocellular

damage are transaminases (AST/ALT) and PT/INR (reflecting synthetic

dysfunction).

•

Bilirubin elevation (jaundice) comes later once hepatocellular necrosis
impairs

bilirubin conjugation and excretion.

•

ALP: usually normal or mildly elevated, not a hallmark of acute
paracetamol

damage.

•

Albumin: has a long half-life (\~20 days), so not an early marker in
acute

overdose.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

INR/PT → can become deranged early as synthetic dysfunction develops.

•

Albumin → won't fall immediately, but the question asks, "most likely
NOT

elevated." Albumin is measured as a concentration (not typically
elevated

anyway).

•

AST → rises early in paracetamol hepatotoxicity.

•

ALP → less sensitive, but can rise later; still bilirubin is more
clearly not

elevated today

Final Answer: Bilirubin (not elevated in the acute phase of paracetamol
overdose).

Paracetamol Overdose: Timeline of Laboratory Changes

Time from

Overdose

Clinical Features Key Biochemical Changes

0--24h (Phase

I\)

Often asymptomatic, or mild GI upset

(nausea, vomiting, malaise).

LFTs (AST/ALT): Normal or just beginning to rise. - INR/PT: Normal.

Bilirubin: Normal. - Albumin: Normal (long half-life).

24--72h

(Phase II)

Right upper quadrant pain,

nausea/vomiting worsen. Hepatic

tenderness.

AST/ALT: Rapid rise (can be \>1000 IU/L). -

INR/PT: Prolonged

(synthetic dysfunction). - Bilirubin: Usually still normal/slightly ↑.
-

Creatinine: May rise (hepatorenal).

72--96h

(Phase III)

Fulminant hepatic failure: jaundice,

coagulopathy, encephalopathy,

hypoglycaemia.

AST/ALT: Peak, then may fall (if massive necrosis). - INR/PT:

Markedly prolonged. - \*\*Bilirubin: ↑↑ (jaundice appears). - Lactate
↑

(poor prognosis).

96h (Phase

IV\)

Recovery or progression to multi-organ

failure/death.

If recovery: labs slowly return to normal. - If

failure: persistent

coagulopathy, hyperbilirubinemia, ↑ creatinine.

High-Yield Pearls for MRCP

•

Earliest marker of severe hepatotoxicity = rise in INR/PT.

•

AST/ALT rise before bilirubin (hepatocellular necrosis precedes
jaundice).

•

Albumin not helpful acutely (long half-life, falls only in chronic
disease).

•

N-acetylcysteine (NAC) most effective if given within 8--10 hours.

BACKUP SCENARION

A 17-year-old female, 36 hours after ingestion of 40 g paracetamol.

Which parameter is most likely normal at presentation?

A. Prothrombin time

B. Serum alanine aminotransferase

C. Serum albumin

D. Serum alkaline phosphatase

E. Serum total bilirubin

ANSWERS:

Serum albumin

Correct Answer:

C. Serum albumin

Key Points from the Scenario

•

17-year-old female

•

36h after paracetamol overdose (40g) → this is well beyond 24h, so
already

in Phase II--III toxicity.

•

At this stage, hepatocellular necrosis is occurring.

•

AST/ALT (transaminases) → already markedly ↑.

•

Prothrombin time (PT) → one of the earliest and most sensitive
indicators

of liver failure → often prolonged by 36h.

•

Bilirubin → rises later (usually \>72h), but may start to climb.

•

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) → can be mildly abnormal, though not the

hallmark.

•

Albumin → has a long half-life (\~20 days), so in acute liver failure it

remains normal early; only in chronic liver disease does it fall.

Detailed Explanation

•

Paracetamol overdose causes centrilobular

hepatic necrosis.

•

Timeline of labs:

o

0--24h: AST/ALT, PT normal.

o

24--72h: ↑AST/ALT, ↑PT.

o

72--96h: ↑↑bilirubin, worsening coagulopathy, encephalopathy.

Albumin won't drop acutely because the liver's existing protein stores
and long

half-life buffer against rapid change.

Why Other Options Are Less Likely

•

A. Prothrombin time → abnormal by 36h (synthetic failure).

•

B. ALT → significantly raised by 36h.

•

D. ALP → can rise, though not specific; not guaranteed normal at this
stage.

•

E. Bilirubin → usually rises later, but may already be mildly abnormal
by 36h.

•

C. Albumin → most definitely still normal.

stem: COPD patient on inhaler Which one increases the chance of pneumonia?
explanation:
Key Points from the Scenario

•

COPD patient on inhaler -- common drugs include bronchodilators,

mucolytics, corticosteroids.

•

Question asks: Which increases chance of pneumonia?

•

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are well known to increase risk of
pneumonia

in COPD (esp. fluticasone \> budesonide).

Oral steroids (prednisolone) also increase immunosuppression, making

pneumonia more likely.

•

Carbocysteine = mucolytic, helps sputum clearance, no pneumonia risk.

•

Theophylline = bronchodilator, narrow therapeutic index, but not linked
to

pneumonia.

Detailed Explanation

•

Prednisolone (systemic steroid):

o

Suppresses immune function.

o

Reduces host defence against infections, including bacterial

pneumonia.

o

ICS in COPD also linked with higher incidence of pneumonia, shown in

TORCH trial.

•

Carbocysteine (mucolytic):

o

Breaks down mucus, improves clearance.

o

No increased risk of pneumonia; may reduce exacerbations.

•

Theophylline (xanthine bronchodilator):

o

Causes arrhythmia, nausea, seizures in toxicity.

o

Not associated with pneumonia risk.

Final Answer:

Prednisolone (or more generally, corticosteroids increase pneumonia risk
in COPD).

BACKUP SCENARION

Asthmatic patient on inhaler

There is consolidation in the lower lobe of the right lung.

Which one increases the chance of pneumonia?

Carbocysteine

Theophylline

Salmeterol

Fluticasone

ANSWERS:

Fluticasone

C. Histones → proteins around which DNA is wrapped; unrelated to
splicing.

•

E. Promoters → regulatory DNA sequences for transcription initiation;
not

removed in splicing.

o

o

Ipsilateral facial sensory loss (CN V nucleus involvement).
